questions.explanation: taciturn. Taciturn means habitually silent or reluctant to speak — fits “answering only in single words.” Garrulous and verbose both mean excessively talkative, the opposite. Eloquent means fluent and persuasive in speech, not about quantity of speech.
questions.stem: Despite being surrounded by chatty relatives, Arjun remained his usual _______ self, answering only in single words.

options.A: garrulous
options.B: taciturn
options.C: eloquent
options.D: verbose

questions.explanation: garrulous. Garrulous means excessively talkative. Laconic and succinct both mean using very few words — opposite of the three-hour lecture. Reticent means reserved in speech.
questions.stem: The professor’s _______ lecturing style — three hours without a single pause — exhausted even his most dedicated students.

options.A: laconic
options.B: succinct
options.C: garrulous
options.D: reticent

questions.explanation: laconic. Laconic means using very few words, terse. The other three options all mean talkative.
questions.stem: Her _______ reply — just “no” — left no room for further discussion.

options.A: verbose
options.B: laconic
options.C: loquacious
options.D: voluble

questions.explanation: equivocal. Equivocal means deliberately ambiguous or vague to avoid commitment. Candid, forthright, and unambiguous all mean the opposite — direct and clear.
questions.stem: The politician’s _______ answer avoided directly confirming or denying the allegation.

options.A: candid
options.B: forthright
options.C: equivocal
options.D: unambiguous

questions.explanation: candid. Candid means open and honest, straightforward. The contrast clue (“unlike his brother’s guarded answers”) signals the opposite of evasive/circumspect/equivocal.
questions.stem: Unlike his brother’s guarded answers, Rohan was refreshingly _______, admitting his mistake without hesitation.

options.A: evasive
options.B: candid
options.C: equivocal
options.D: circumspect

questions.explanation: circumlocution. Circumlocution means using many words where fewer would do, especially to avoid saying something directly. Fits “never quite saying what everyone knew.”
questions.stem: The ambassador’s speech was full of _______, never quite saying what everyone knew he meant.

options.A: circumlocution
options.B: brevity
options.C: candor
options.D: bluntness

questions.explanation: eloquence. Eloquence means fluent, persuasive speaking ability — matches “gifted orator” and “persuaded.”
questions.stem: A gifted orator, she could speak with such _______ that even hostile audiences found themselves persuaded.

options.A: ineloquence
options.B: eloquence
options.C: taciturnity
options.D: reticence

questions.explanation: prevaricating. To prevaricate is to speak evasively or misleadingly, often to avoid the truth or delay stating one’s real point.
questions.stem: He has a habit of _______ — talking around a topic for ten minutes before ever stating his actual point.

options.A: prevaricating
options.B: elaborating
options.C: clarifying
options.D: summarizing

questions.explanation: voluble. Voluble means speaking rapidly and fluently, talkative — fits needing her to “slow down.”
questions.stem: The witness’s testimony was so _______ that the lawyer had to ask her to slow down and repeat herself.

options.A: terse
options.B: voluble
options.C: reticent
options.D: laconic

questions.explanation: vague. Vague means lacking clarity or precision — fits “satisfied no one” as a non-answer. The other three all mean clear and direct.
questions.stem: Rather than answer directly, the CEO gave a _______ statement that satisfied no one.

options.A: forthright
options.B: vague
options.C: explicit
options.D: transparent

questions.explanation: scathing. Scathing means harshly critical — matches the devastating emotional effect described.
questions.stem: The critic’s _______ review left the young author in tears, questioning whether she should ever write again.

options.A: laudatory
options.B: scathing
options.C: tepid
options.D: glowing

questions.explanation: laudatory. Laudatory means expressing praise. Fits “praising its ambition.”
questions.stem: Despite the film’s flaws, most reviewers were _______, praising its ambition and visual style.

options.A: laudatory
options.B: scathing
options.C: derisive
options.D: contemptuous

questions.explanation: tepid. Tepid means lukewarm, showing little enthusiasm — fits “neither strongly positive nor negative.”
questions.stem: The teacher’s feedback was _______ — neither strongly positive nor negative, just a list of minor observations.

options.A: scathing
options.B: laudatory
options.C: tepid
options.D: glowing

questions.explanation: disdainful. Disdainful means showing contempt or scorn — fits “refusing to dignify it,” which implies looking down on the criticism.
questions.stem: He responded to the criticism with _______ silence, refusing to dignify it with a reply.

options.A: disdainful
options.B: admiring
options.C: grateful
options.D: appreciative

questions.explanation: grudging. Grudging means given reluctantly or unwillingly — fits “reluctant but unwilling to reject.”
questions.stem: The board gave the proposal only _______ approval, clearly reluctant but unwilling to reject it outright.

options.A: enthusiastic
options.B: grudging
options.C: wholehearted
options.D: unqualified

questions.explanation: disparage. Disparage means to belittle or criticize dismissively — fits the contrast with privately thinking it was excellent.
questions.stem: She was quick to _______ her colleague’s work in meetings, but privately admitted it was excellent.

options.A: commend
options.B: extol
options.C: disparage
options.D: applaud

questions.explanation: exasperation. Exasperation means a feeling of intense irritation mixed with frustration/resignation — closest match to “resigned disappointment.”
questions.stem: The reviewer’s tone was one of _______ — a kind of resigned disappointment rather than outright anger.

options.A: fury
options.B: exuberance
options.C: exasperation
options.D: elation

questions.explanation: perfunctory. Perfunctory means done as a routine or minimum obligation, without real interest — fits “polite, but not enthusiastic.”
questions.stem: His speech was met with _______ applause — polite, but clearly not enthusiastic.

options.A: rapturous
options.B: perfunctory
options.C: thunderous
options.D: unanimous

questions.explanation: censure. Censure means strong formal or public criticism — fits criticism of crisis “handling,” implied to be poor.
questions.stem: The critics were unanimous in their _______ of the government’s handling of the crisis.

options.A: commendation
options.B: censure
options.C: endorsement
options.D: approval

questions.explanation: sycophantic. Sycophantic means excessively flattering toward someone in order to gain advantage — fits “aimed at winning favor.”
questions.stem: Rather than genuine admiration, his compliments seemed like _______ flattery aimed at winning favor.

options.A: sincere
options.B: heartfelt
options.C: sycophantic
options.D: candid

questions.explanation: mercurial. Mercurial means subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood — fits “cheerful one moment, sullen the next” exactly.
questions.stem: His _______ moods made him unpredictable — cheerful one moment, sullen the next.

options.A: stable
options.B: mercurial
options.C: placid
options.D: staid

questions.explanation: placid. Placid means calm and unruffled — fits “unmoved by the panic.”
questions.stem: Despite the chaos around her, she remained _______, unmoved by the panic of others.

options.A: volatile
options.B: placid
options.C: mercurial
options.D: excitable

questions.stem: His _______ pursuit of the goal, despite repeated setbacks, eventually paid off.

options.A: fickle
options.B: tenacious
options.C: capricious
options.D: desultory

questions.stem: Her _______ decisions — changing plans on a whim almost daily — frustrated the whole team.

options.A: resolute
options.B: steadfast
options.C: capricious
options.D: tenacious

questions.stem: Even as a young officer, he displayed remarkable _______ in the face of enemy fire.

options.A: temerity
options.B: timidity
options.C: diffidence
options.D: trepidation

questions.stem: His _______ manner in front of his superiors — never volunteering an opinion, always deferring — held back his career.

options.A: audacious
options.B: diffident
options.C: brazen
options.D: assertive

questions.stem: The new intern’s _______ attitude — questioning senior managers openly on his first day — shocked the office.

options.A: diffident
options.B: reticent
options.C: brazen
options.D: demure

options.A: miserly

options.A: magnanimous
options.B: vindictive

options.D: altruistic

questions.stem: She approached every decision with cool, _______ reasoning, rarely swayed by emotion.

options.A: impetuous
options.B: pragmatic
options.C: mercurial
options.D: capricious

options.A: cursory
options.B: meticulous
options.C: perfunctory
options.D: superficial

options.A: meticulous

options.A: desultory

options.D: languid

options.A: rigorous
options.B: diligent

options.D: assiduous

options.A: industrious
options.B: lethargic

options.D: vigorous

options.A: perfunctory

options.A: industrious
options.B: indolent
options.C: diligent
options.D: assiduous

options.A: haphazard
options.B: rigorous
options.C: cursory
options.D: desultory

options.C: incessant

options.B: perennial
options.C: fleeting
options.D: momentary

options.A: constant
options.B: intermittent
options.C: uninterrupted
options.D: continuous

options.A: rampant
options.B: rare
options.C: contained
options.D: isolated

questions.stem: The volatile currency made prices _______ — nobody could predict what anything would cost a week ahead.

options.A: stable
options.B: erratic
options.C: fixed
options.D: predictable

options.A: transient
options.B: fleeting
options.C: persistent
options.D: momentary

options.A: exacerbate

options.D: intensify

options.A: mitigate
options.B: alleviate
options.C: exacerbate
options.D: diminish

options.A: exacerbate
options.B: mitigate
options.C: intensify
options.D: aggravate

options.A: catalyst

options.A: impede

options.D: obstruct

options.A: volatile
options.B: dynamic
options.C: static
options.D: turbulent

options.A: static
options.B: dynamic
options.C: inert
options.D: dormant

questions.stem: The committee’s report was the _______ for the sweeping changes that followed in the industry.

options.A: impetus
options.B: hindrance
options.C: deterrent
options.D: obstruction

options.A: salubrious
options.B: beneficial
options.C: deleterious
options.D: salutary

options.C: candid

options.A: evasive
options.B: forthright
options.C: equivocal
options.D: devious

options.A: convincing

options.D: candid

questions.stem: Her _______ manner toward her boss — constant compliments, exaggerated laughter at his jokes — embarrassed her colleagues.

options.A: obsequious
options.B: candid
options.C: forthright
options.D: blunt

questions.stem: The whistleblower’s motives were entirely _______ — she gained nothing personally from the disclosure.

options.A: mercenary

options.D: opportunistic

questions.stem: His decision to switch parties just before the election, purely to secure a ministerial post, was widely seen as _______.

options.A: principled

options.C: opportunistic
options.D: selfless

options.A: genuine

options.D: unplanned

options.A: plausible
options.B: blatant

options.D: credible

options.A: substance
options.B: tokenism
options.C: commitment
options.D: reform

options.A: lavish

options.B: parsimonious

options.A: lavish
options.B: austerity

options.A: austere
options.B: frugal
options.C: ostentatious

options.A: ostentatious

options.D: opulent

options.A: austere

options.C: opulent
options.D: minimalist

options.A: profligate
options.B: judicious

options.D: wasteful

options.C: understated

options.A: mainstream

options.C: esoteric
options.D: popular

options.A: unambiguous

options.A: discord

questions.stem: The startup had raised three rounds of funding on the strength of a single charismatic pitch, with revenue numbers that were, in hindsight, wildly optimistic. Investors, dazzled by the founder’s confidence, rarely asked for independent verification of the figures. When the company finally collapsed, the postmortem made clear that _______

options.A: the founder had committed no wrongdoing whatsoever.
options.B: due diligence had been sacrificed for excitement about the founder’s vision.
options.C: all startups with charismatic founders are destined to fail.
options.D: revenue projections are impossible to verify in any industry.

questions.explanation: Follows the paragraph’s setup — a bet on tourism as a replacement — to its logical payoff. (A) contradicts the premise that stocks had collapsed and the town needed an alternative. (C) contradicts investing in coastline tourism. (D) introduces an irrelevant claim about other towns.
questions.stem: For years, the coastal town relied on a single fishing fleet for most of its income. When stocks collapsed after decades of overfishing, the town faced a choice: diversify or decline. Local leaders invested heavily in tourism infrastructure, betting that the same coastline that once fed the fishing industry could now attract visitors instead. A decade later, _______

options.A: the fishing industry had fully recovered to its former size.
options.B: tourism revenue had come to exceed what the fishing industry once provided.
options.C: the town had abandoned the coastline entirely for inland development.
options.D: no other coastal towns had attempted a similar transition.

questions.explanation: Follows directly from the procedural change described — breaking the proposal into clauses reducing friction. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the constructive tone the paragraph has built toward.
questions.stem: The committee had debated the proposal for nearly two years without resolution, each side convinced the other was arguing in bad faith. When a new chairperson took over, she made a small but crucial change: rather than voting on the entire proposal, members would vote on each clause separately. Within a single meeting, _______

options.A: the committee was permanently disbanded.
options.B: most clauses were approved with far less friction than expected.
options.C: the original proposal was rejected without any amendments.
options.D: the new chairperson resigned over the dispute.

questions.explanation: Matches the described middle-ground fix exactly — keep new layout, restore missed shortcuts. (A) and (D) contradict the compromise described. (C) contradicts the team’s stated responsiveness to feedback.
questions.stem: Early users of the app complained loudly about a redesigned interface that removed several familiar shortcuts. The development team, initially defensive, eventually sat down to review months of user feedback in detail. Rather than reverting the design entirely, they restored the specific shortcuts users had missed most while keeping the new visual layout. The result was _______

options.A: a near-total abandonment of the app by its user base.
options.B: a version that retained the redesign’s benefits while addressing the core complaints.
options.C: a decision to ignore all future user feedback.
options.D: a complete return to the original, pre-redesign interface.

questions.explanation: “Something curators hadn’t anticipated” signals a surprising, specific finding — this option gives a concrete, unexpected behavior. (A) is plausible but contradicts the “hadn’t anticipated” framing pointing toward something more specific. (B) is too vague to be “something” specific. (D) introduces an unrelated, unsupported claim.
questions.stem: The museum’s new policy allowed visitors to photograph any exhibit except a small number of light-sensitive manuscripts. Initially, curators worried this would encourage crowding and reduce the quality of the viewing experience for others. Attendance data from the first year, however, showed something curators hadn’t anticipated: _______

options.A: visitors spent less time overall in the museum than before.
options.B: photography privileges had no measurable effect on visitor behavior.
options.C: many visitors lingered longer, using photographs to study details more closely.
options.D: the manuscripts had to be removed from display entirely.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the setup — backchannel drafting designed to avoid either side “formally proposing” a compromise, which naturally resolves into a face-saving deal. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the constructive purpose described for the backchannel effort.
questions.stem: The negotiations had stalled for months over a single disputed clause about intellectual property rights. Both delegations publicly insisted they would not compromise. Behind closed doors, however, junior staff on both sides had quietly begun drafting alternative language that neither side had to formally propose first. This backchannel work eventually _______

options.A: had no impact on the final outcome of the talks.
options.B: provided the face-saving compromise that broke the public deadlock.
options.C: was rejected by both delegations as irrelevant.
options.D: led to the complete collapse of the negotiations.

questions.explanation: Follows directly from the diagnosis — the issue was the rubric, not the content, so fixing the rubric should improve outcomes without changing difficulty. (A) contradicts the fix having any effect. (C) and (D) are unsupported and contradict the corrective direction of the paragraph.
questions.stem: The professor’s course had a reputation for being nearly impossible to pass, and enrollment had dwindled for years as a result. When a new dean reviewed the syllabus, she found the material wasn’t actually harder than comparable courses — the grading rubric was simply unusually punitive for minor errors. After the rubric was revised, _______

options.A: enrollment continued to decline at the same rate as before.
options.B: pass rates rose without any change to course content or difficulty.
options.C: the course was removed from the curriculum entirely.
options.D: the professor was asked to make the material more difficult.

questions.explanation: Matches the paragraph’s setup of skepticism giving way to a successful, resource-saving adaptation. (A) contradicts a positive outcome the paragraph is building toward. (C) contradicts adopting the new method successfully. (D) is an unsupported new claim.
questions.stem: The vineyard had used the same irrigation method for three generations, drawing water from a nearby river regardless of seasonal rainfall. A prolonged drought forced the owners to install sensors that adjusted watering based on real-time soil moisture. Skeptical at first, the family found that within two seasons, _______

options.A: grape yields collapsed due to insufficient water.
options.B: water usage dropped substantially while yields held steady or improved.
options.C: they abandoned the sensors and returned to the old method.
options.D: the vineyard shifted entirely to a different crop.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the described improvement — reliable information addressing the original complaint about unpredictability. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the positive, problem-solving direction the paragraph has been building.
questions.stem: The city’s bus system had long been criticized for unpredictable arrival times, with riders often waiting without any real information. A pilot program installed GPS trackers on a quarter of the fleet and published real-time arrival estimates through a simple app. Ridership on those specific routes _______

options.A: dropped noticeably as riders switched to other forms of transport.
options.B: rose, as riders reported feeling more confident planning their trips.
options.C: remained completely unaffected by the change.
options.D: fell because the app was too complicated to use.

questions.explanation: Stays tightly within the paragraph’s established theme — ambiguity as a strength because it reflects how memory actually works. (A) contradicts the deliberate ambiguity being praised. (C) and (D) introduce unrelated new information about sales and future work.
questions.stem: The novel’s central theme is the unreliability of memory — every character remembers the same pivotal event differently, and the author deliberately never resolves whose version is “true.” Critics have praised this ambiguity as the book’s greatest strength, arguing that _______

options.A: the author should have included a clear timeline of events.
options.B: it mirrors how memory itself functions in real life.
options.C: the book’s sales figures exceeded the publisher’s expectations.
options.D: the author’s next novel will explore a similar theme.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the “rather than limiting creativity” setup — the constraint became a source of inventiveness. (B) directly contradicts the local-sourcing premise. (C) and (D) introduce unrelated new facts not set up by the paragraph.
questions.stem: The chef’s tasting menu is built entirely around ingredients sourced within a fifty-kilometer radius of the restaurant, changing weekly based on what local farms have available. This constraint, rather than limiting creativity, has _______

options.A: forced the kitchen to develop unusually inventive combinations.
options.B: led the restaurant to import ingredients from overseas instead.
options.C: resulted in the restaurant closing during the winter months.
options.D: prompted a rival restaurant to adopt a similar sourcing policy.

questions.explanation: Follows directly from the successful restoration and reinforcement described. (A) contradicts a successful restoration outcome. (C) and (D) introduce new, unsupported claims not implied by the paragraph.
questions.stem: The city’s oldest bridge, built in 1889, was scheduled for demolition after engineers deemed it structurally unsound. A local preservation group raised funds not to demolish it, but to fully restore its original ironwork while reinforcing the foundation to modern safety standards. Today, the bridge _______

options.A: remains closed to all traffic pending further review.
options.B: carries both pedestrian and vehicle traffic safely.
options.C: has been relocated to a museum for public display.
options.D: is being considered for a second, unrelated renovation project.

questions.explanation: Reasonable, paragraph-consistent continuation — a “controversial decision” plausibly produces divided opinion, which surveys would capture. (A) is an extreme overreach not indicated. (C) and (D) introduce unrelated new information about pricing and other orchestras.
questions.stem: The orchestra’s new music director made a controversial decision in her first season: eliminating the traditional intermission from every performance. She argued that unbroken performances preserved the emotional continuity that composers originally intended. Season ticket holder surveys later showed _______

options.A: most patrons had stopped attending performances altogether.
options.B: audiences were fairly evenly split, with strong opinions on both sides.
options.C: the orchestra’s ticket prices had increased significantly.
options.D: a rival orchestra had adopted the opposite policy.

questions.explanation: Stays tied to the paragraph’s core thread — the delay caused by slow trial recruitment, and its consequence within the same competitive space (treatments for the same condition). (A), (C), and (D) all pivot to information the paragraph gave no basis to expect.
questions.stem: The biotech firm’s flagship drug had shown remarkable results in early trials, curing a rare condition in nearly ninety percent of patients. But the condition was so rare that recruiting enough patients for a full-scale trial took years longer than expected. By the time the drug finally reached regulators, _______

options.A: a competitor’s drug for an unrelated condition had already launched.
options.B: two other companies had developed treatments for the same condition.
options.C: the original research team had moved on to a different project entirely.
options.D: the company’s stock price had become entirely disconnected from the drug’s prospects.

questions.explanation: A natural, paragraph-consistent consequence of a small publisher having a surprise bestseller — larger publishers taking notice. (B) contradicts the implied credit the small house’s translation choices deserve. (C) contradicts the pattern the house is known for. (D) introduces an unsupported, unrelated legal claim.
questions.stem: The small publishing house built its reputation on translating obscure foreign-language novels that larger publishers considered too risky. One such gamble, a debut novel from a little-known Icelandic author, unexpectedly became an international bestseller. The unexpected success _______

options.A: prompted several larger publishers to bid for the house itself.
options.B: had nothing to do with the quality of the translation.
options.C: discouraged the house from continuing to take similar risks.
options.D: led the original Icelandic publisher to file a lawsuit.

questions.explanation: Follows directly from the described relocation and its intended purpose. (A) and (C) contradict a successful correction. (D) introduces an unsupported claim — the paragraph never suggests wealthy areas lost stations, only that new ones were added elsewhere.
questions.stem: The city’s new bike-share program was initially criticized for placing docking stations disproportionately in wealthier neighborhoods. After a public outcry, the operator committed to relocating a quarter of all stations to underserved areas within a year. By the following summer, ridership data showed _______

options.A: overall program usage had declined sharply.
options.B: meaningful growth in ridership specifically from the newly served neighborhoods.
options.C: the program had been shut down due to funding issues.
options.D: wealthier neighborhoods had lost access to the program entirely.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the narrative tension the paragraph builds — near-abandonment followed by a last-chance payoff. (A), (C), and (D) all break from the story’s established trajectory with unrelated pivots.
questions.stem: The documentary crew had planned to spend two weeks filming a single elusive species of owl. After nearly ten days without a single sighting, they were prepared to abandon the project. On their final scheduled night, _______

options.A: they decided to focus the documentary on a different species instead.
options.B: they finally captured rare footage of the owl hunting.
options.C: the production company canceled their funding.
options.D: a separate research team announced the species was extinct.

questions.explanation: Follows the “instead” signal directly — using its established strength (route familiarity) to compete effectively, contradicting the analysts’ prediction. (A) and (C) match the analysts’ prediction rather than contradicting it as “instead” requires. (D) introduces an unrelated new business direction.
questions.stem: The regional airline had built its entire business model around routes too small for major carriers to bother with. When a larger competitor unexpectedly entered one of its core markets, most analysts predicted the smaller airline would struggle to survive. Instead, its deep familiarity with the route’s specific demand patterns allowed it to _______

options.A: exit the market entirely within six months.
options.B: undercut the larger competitor on the routes that mattered most.
options.C: merge with the larger competitor soon after.
options.D: expand into international long-haul routes for the first time.

questions.explanation: Fits the buildup toward a significant, specific discovery within the same site. (A) overreaches — a chamber doesn’t necessarily mean total misidentification. (C) and (D) introduce unrelated new information about funding or a separate site.
questions.stem: The archaeological team had spent three seasons excavating a site they believed to be a minor trading post. A chance discovery of a sealed underground chamber in the final week of the third season revealed _______

options.A: that the site had been misidentified as a trading post entirely.
options.B: a burial complex far more elaborate than anything expected at the site.
options.C: that the team’s funding would be renewed for a fourth season.
options.D: an unrelated site nearby that had never been surveyed.

questions.explanation: Matches the established measured, balanced tone. (A) and (C)/(D) are all extreme, one-sided judgments the paragraph’s tone explicitly rules out.
questions.stem: The critic’s essay on the film was measured throughout, acknowledging both its technical brilliance and its narrative shortcomings without ever tipping fully into praise or condemnation. Its final line captured this balance precisely: _______

options.A: “a masterpiece that redefines the genre for a new generation.”
options.B: “a flawed but genuinely worthwhile two hours at the cinema.”
options.C: “a complete waste of the audience’s time and money.”
options.D: “the single worst film released this decade.”

questions.explanation: Matches the described restraint — probabilistic, non-catastrophizing, and still emphasizing agency (“with immediate global action”). (A) and (D) are catastrophizing extremes the paragraph explicitly says she avoids. (C) contradicts her position as a climate scientist entirely.
questions.stem: The scientist’s popular book on climate modeling is notable for its restraint — she resists the temptation to catastrophize, presenting probabilities and ranges rather than certainties. Even in her concluding chapter, she writes only that _______

options.A: civilization as we know it will certainly collapse within decades.
options.B: the coming changes are likely to be manageable with immediate global action.
options.C: climate change is a hoax perpetuated by uninformed activists.
options.D: nothing meaningful can be done to change the outcome now.

questions.explanation: Matches the modest, understated tone described. (A) is grandiose, contradicting “understated.” (C) and (D) are dramatically negative, also contradicting the calm, reflective tone.
questions.stem: The retiring judge’s farewell speech was notably understated for someone with four decades on the bench — no dramatic pronouncements, just a quiet reflection on the weight of ordinary decisions. She closed simply by saying that _______

options.A: her career had been the greatest achievement in the history of the judiciary.
options.B: she hoped she had, in most cases, gotten it right.
options.C: the legal system was fundamentally broken beyond repair.
options.D: she regretted every decision she had made on the bench.

questions.explanation: Matches the described plain, unadorned, unromantic style. (A), (C), and (D) all use exactly the exoticizing, mystical language the paragraph says the writer deliberately avoided.
questions.stem: The travel writer’s account of the remote village was deliberately unromantic, avoiding the exoticizing language common to the genre and instead describing daily life with plain, unadorned observation. Of the village’s famous festival, she wrote only that _______

options.A: it was the most magical, otherworldly spectacle imaginable.
options.B: it was well-attended and lasted most of the afternoon.
options.C: no outsider could ever truly understand its ancient mysteries.
options.D: it transported visitors to another realm entirely.

questions.explanation: Matches the described directness and rejection of corporate euphemism. (A) and (C) are exactly the euphemistic corporate language the paragraph says she avoided. (D) contradicts the fact that layoffs were happening at all.
questions.stem: The startup founder’s internal memo announcing layoffs was unusually direct, avoiding corporate euphemism in favor of plain acknowledgment of the human cost. Rather than describing it as “rightsizing” or “restructuring,” she wrote that the company _______

options.A: was undergoing an exciting strategic realignment for the future.
options.B: was letting people go, and that this decision would hurt real families.
options.C: was implementing synergistic efficiencies across all departments.
options.D: remained fully committed to its existing headcount targets.

questions.explanation: Matches the “admiring but not uncritical” balance described. (A) is uncritical celebration, (D) is pure condemnation — both contradict the stated balance. (C) contradicts “undeniable political skill,” which implies real significance.
questions.stem: The historian’s tone throughout the biography is admiring but not uncritical — she credits her subject’s undeniable political skill while refusing to excuse his documented cruelties. Her final assessment describes him as _______

options.A: an unblemished hero whose legacy deserves nothing but celebration.
options.B: a man whose considerable talents were inseparable from his considerable flaws.
options.C: an unremarkable figure whose importance has been vastly overstated.
options.D: a villain with no redeeming qualities whatsoever.

questions.explanation: Matches “dry, understated humor” exactly — a mildly deflating comparison rather than outright mockery. (A) is outright mockery/exaggeration, contradicting “understated.” (C) and (D) contradict “clearly dislikes.”
questions.stem: The tech reviewer’s writing style is famous for dry, understated humor rather than outright mockery, even when reviewing a product she clearly dislikes. Summing up the disappointing new phone, she wrote that it was _______

options.A: an unmitigated, catastrophic disaster unfit for human use.
options.B: fine, in the way a slightly stale sandwich is fine.
options.C: the greatest technological achievement of the decade.
options.D: something she would recommend to absolutely everyone.

questions.explanation: Matches the described shift to “stark, minimal language.” (A) and (D) contradict this shift by describing increased complexity. (C) introduces an unrelated, unsupported genre change.
questions.stem: The poet’s later work abandoned the ornate, elaborate style of his early career in favor of stark, minimal language. Reviewers noted that even his poems about grief, once dense with metaphor, had become _______

options.A: even more elaborately metaphorical than before.
options.B: spare, direct, and almost unbearably plain.
options.C: entirely abandoned in favor of prose fiction.
options.D: longer and more structurally complex than his early work.

questions.explanation: Matches the described hedging and acknowledgment of uncertainty. (A), (C), and (D) all state unwarranted certainty, contradicting the entire premise of the paragraph.
questions.stem: The economist’s testimony before the committee was carefully hedged throughout, qualifying nearly every claim with acknowledgment of uncertainty. Asked directly whether a recession was coming, she would say only that _______

options.A: a recession was absolutely certain within the next two quarters.
options.B: the risk had risen, though the timing remained genuinely uncertain.
options.C: no recession would ever occur again in the modern economy.
options.D: she personally guaranteed the economy would avoid any downturn.

questions.explanation: Matches the described “flat, clinical detail” avoiding melodrama. (A) is melodramatic, contradicting the stated style. (C) imposes the “redemption-narrative” framing the paragraph says the book avoids. (D) contradicts the fact that she is, per the paragraph, describing it.
questions.stem: Unlike most memoirs about addiction, this one avoids both melodrama and redemption-narrative clichés, presenting the author’s relapses with the same flat, clinical detail as her recoveries. She describes her lowest point not with anguish, but simply as _______

options.A: the most devastating, soul-crushing tragedy imaginable.
options.B: a period that, factually, lasted about four months.
options.C: a triumphant turning point on her path to healing.
options.D: something she refuses to discuss even now.

questions.explanation: Consistent with the explicit warning against inferring causation from correlation. (A) and (C) directly contradict that warning. (D) makes no sense given the report is precisely about these findings.
questions.stem: The report’s authors were careful to note that correlation between the two economic indicators, while statistically strong, does not by itself establish causation. Any policy recommendation based solely on this data, they warned, would be _______

options.A: fully justified by the strength of the statistical relationship.
options.B: premature without further investigation into the underlying mechanism.
options.C: guaranteed to succeed regardless of the causal relationship.
options.D: unrelated to the report’s own findings.

questions.explanation: The word “however” signals a contradiction to the official statement — engineers already knew about it as a safety risk well before the “precautionary” recall. (A) doesn’t contradict the official line at all. (C) undercuts rather than supports the implied contradiction (a safety story needs a safety flag, not a cosmetic one). (D) is irrelevant to the specific defect in question.
questions.stem: The company’s official statement insisted that the product recall was purely precautionary, with no confirmed reports of the defect causing harm. Internal emails later revealed, however, that engineers had flagged the exact same defect _______

options.A: only after the recall had already been announced.
options.B: as a known safety risk more than a year earlier.
options.C: as a minor cosmetic issue unrelated to safety.
options.D: in a completely different, unrelated product line.

questions.explanation: “Ignoring this caveat” signals the media did exactly what the authors warned against — overgeneralizing. (A) and (D) would mean the media respected the caveat, contradicting “ignoring.” (C) is an overcorrection not indicated by the sentence.
questions.stem: The study’s authors explicitly stated that their sample, drawn entirely from one urban university, could not be assumed to represent the broader population. Subsequent media coverage, ignoring this caveat, described the findings as _______

options.A: applicable only to the specific group studied, as intended.
options.B: universally true of all young adults everywhere.
options.C: too limited to draw any conclusions from at all.
options.D: consistent with the authors’ own stated caveats.

questions.explanation: Consistent with the setup — if physical evidence was inconclusive, a verdict would logically lean more on testimony. (A) contradicts evidence being considered at all in reaching any verdict. (C) contradicts the premise that physical evidence alone was insufficient. (D) directly contradicts “eleven hours of deliberation” already stated.
questions.stem: The defense argued throughout the trial that the physical evidence was inconclusive and could not, on its own, establish guilt. The jury’s verdict, delivered after eleven hours of deliberation, ultimately _______

options.A: fully agreed that no evidence had been considered.
options.B: rested heavily on testimony rather than the physical evidence alone.
options.C: ignored testimony entirely in favor of only physical evidence.
options.D: was reached in under thirty minutes of discussion.

questions.explanation: “However” signals a contradiction to the sweeping claim — a partial, conditional performance directly undercuts “completely waterproof under any conditions” without being an absolute reversal (D would be too extreme given “waterproof” fabrics are rarely entirely non-resistant). (A) and (C) don’t contradict the claim at all.
questions.stem: The manufacturer claimed its new fabric was completely waterproof under any conditions. Independent lab tests, however, found that the material _______

options.A: performed exactly as the manufacturer had claimed in every scenario.
options.B: resisted light rain but failed under sustained heavy exposure.
options.C: was even more waterproof than advertised.
options.D: had no water-resistant properties detected in testing.

questions.explanation: Fits the setup of an audit revealing a broken promise — public funds involved despite the “no burden on taxpayers” claim. (A) confirms rather than contradicts, missing the point of an audit “finding” something. (C) and (D) are positive, unrelated claims not indicated by the contradiction being set up.
questions.stem: The city council had promised that the new stadium would be funded entirely through private investment, with no burden on taxpayers. An independent financial audit released this week found that _______

options.A: private investment had, in fact, covered the entire project cost.
options.B: public funds had quietly covered nearly a third of construction costs.
options.C: the stadium project had been completed under budget.
options.D: taxpayers had received a partial refund from the project’s profits.

questions.explanation: The structure (“marketing emphasized X… data showed”) signals a contradiction is coming. (A) confirms rather than contradicts the marketing claim. (C) sidesteps the comparison the sentence sets up. (D) is a positive, unrelated claim not indicated by the contrast being built.
questions.stem: The airline’s marketing emphasized an “on-time guarantee” as a key selling point over its competitors. Government transportation data for the same period showed that the airline’s on-time performance was _______

options.A: the best in the industry, exactly as advertised.
options.B: actually below the industry average.
options.C: impossible to measure using available data.
options.D: improving steadily every single month.

questions.explanation: “Later revealed” signals a contradiction to the company’s stated justification — spending more on marketing than R&D undercuts the R&D-cost justification specifically. (A) supports rather than contradicts the company’s claim. (C) is an extreme overreach not indicated. (D) is unrelated to the R&D justification being questioned.
questions.stem: The pharmaceutical company insisted its pricing reflected the enormous cost of research and development. Financial disclosures later revealed that _______

options.A: R&D spending was, in fact, the company’s single largest expense.
options.B: marketing expenditures exceeded R&D spending by a significant margin.
options.C: the company had never invested in research of any kind.
options.D: pricing had remained flat over the disclosed period.

questions.explanation: Fits the “watchdog review found” structure signaling a contradiction — reclassifying spending undercuts the headline figure. (A) confirms rather than contradicts. (C) and (D) are unrelated positive claims not indicated by a critical watchdog review.
questions.stem: The nonprofit’s annual report proudly stated that over ninety percent of donations went directly to program services, with minimal administrative overhead. An independent watchdog’s review of the same financials found that _______

options.A: the ninety percent figure was accurately reported.
options.B: a significant portion of “program services” spending was actually administrative in nature.
options.C: the nonprofit had exceeded its own stated targets.
options.D: donations had increased significantly that year.

questions.explanation: Fits the “investigation revealed” structure signaling a debunking of the menu’s claim. (A) confirms rather than contradicts, undermining the point of an investigative reveal. (C) and (D) are unrelated claims not indicated by the setup.
questions.stem: The restaurant’s menu described the fish as “locally caught that morning.” A journalist’s investigation into the supply chain revealed that _______

options.A: the fish was, in fact, caught locally as described.
options.B: the fish was frozen and shipped from several states away.
options.C: the restaurant had stopped serving fish entirely.
options.D: local fishing had increased significantly in recent years.

questions.explanation: “On balance” signals a weighing of the described trade-off (savings vs. maintenance risk), and a net-positive conclusion fits a company that presumably kept the automation. (B) and (D) are extreme overreactions the paragraph gives no basis for. (C) contradicts the “forty percent” reduction already stated.
questions.stem: The factory’s new automated packing line reduced labor costs by nearly forty percent within its first year. But the same automation required specialized technicians to maintain equipment that occasional breakdowns could halt production for days. On balance, management concluded that _______

options.A: the savings clearly outweighed the new maintenance risks.
options.B: automation should be reversed immediately at all costs.
options.C: labor costs were actually unaffected by the change.
options.D: the factory should close permanently.

questions.explanation: Follows logically from “saturated soil… weakened” plus a final storm — a landslide is the direct, foreseeable consequence. (A) and (D) contradict the described rainy, wet conditions. (C) is unrelated to the disaster being set up.
questions.stem: Heavy rains upstream saturated soil that had already been weakened by months of unrelated construction work. When a final storm hit, the combination proved catastrophic: _______

options.A: the drought conditions worsened significantly.
options.B: a major landslide blocked the only road into the valley.
options.C: construction work was completed ahead of schedule.
options.D: the region experienced an unexpected heat wave.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the stated intent of the policy succeeding as designed — the straightforward, expected outcome given no contradicting signal (“however,” “but”) appears in the sentence. (B) would require a “however” to be a coherent point about unintended consequences, which isn’t set up. (C) and (D) contradict a policy working as intended with no signal of failure.
questions.stem: The new tax incentive was designed to encourage small businesses to hire additional staff. Within eighteen months of its introduction, economic data showed that _______

options.A: small business hiring had increased measurably in eligible sectors.
options.B: large corporations had captured the majority of the incentive’s benefits.
options.C: small business hiring had declined sharply during the same period.
options.D: the incentive had no measurable relationship to business decisions.

questions.explanation: Direct, sensible consequence of severe water scarcity — a forced shift to efficiency. (A) contradicts the scarcity described. (C) contradicts “forced to” respond. (D) is an illogical, unsupported extreme.
questions.stem: The river’s water level dropped to its lowest point in recorded history after three consecutive years of below-average rainfall. Farmers who had long relied on flood irrigation were forced to _______

options.A: increase their reliance on flood irrigation methods.
options.B: adopt more water-efficient irrigation techniques.
options.C: ignore the change in water levels entirely.
options.D: relocate to a region with even less rainfall.

questions.explanation: Direct, logical consequence for companies dependent on precisely-timed, low-buffer inventory when shipping becomes unreliable and expensive. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the described disruption’s direct relevance to such companies.
questions.stem: A sudden drop in global shipping capacity, caused by a shortage of available containers, sent freight costs soaring across every major trade route. Companies dependent on just-in-time inventory models found that _______

options.A: their supply chains were completely unaffected by the shortage.
options.B: delays and cost increases forced a rethink of lean inventory strategies.
options.C: freight costs actually fell as a result of the shortage.
options.D: the shortage had no bearing on inventory planning.

questions.explanation: Direct, sensible next step given the described breakthrough and immediate industry interest. (A) contradicts the enzyme’s described speed advantage. (C) and (D) are unsupported pivots the paragraph gives no basis for.
questions.stem: A newly discovered enzyme was found to break down a common plastic polymer at room temperature, far faster than any previously known method. Waste management companies immediately began exploring whether the enzyme could be _______

options.A: used to slow down existing recycling processes.
options.B: scaled up for industrial-level plastic recycling.
options.C: applied to materials entirely unrelated to plastic.
options.D: banned due to safety concerns about its use.

questions.explanation: “However” plus “speculative asset purchases” points directly to asset-price inflation as the unintended consequence. (A) contradicts “however,” which signals the outcome diverged from intention. (C) contradicts the described flow of new lending having an effect. (D) contradicts a rate cut, which typically increases, not reduces, money supply.
questions.stem: The central bank’s decision to cut interest rates was intended to stimulate borrowing and investment during a period of sluggish growth. Within months, however, most of the new lending had flowed not into productive investment but into speculative asset purchases, _______

options.A: exactly fulfilling the policy’s original intention.
options.B: inflating prices in property and financial markets instead.
options.C: having no measurable effect on any market.
options.D: reducing the money supply significantly.

questions.explanation: Direct, logical consequence of aging infrastructure facing unprecedented sustained demand. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the described strain and the phrase “never designed for such sustained peak load.”
questions.stem: A prolonged heatwave pushed electricity demand for air conditioning to record levels across the grid. Several aging power plants, never designed for such sustained peak load, _______

options.A: operated at their lowest capacity in years.
options.B: experienced unexpected outages during the peak demand period.
options.C: were entirely unaffected by the increased demand.
options.D: reduced their output deliberately to save costs.

questions.explanation: Directly follows from unbundling’s known consumer friction — the gap between advertised base fare and actual final cost. (A) contradicts the stated purpose of a lower advertised fare. (C) and (D) are unrelated to the complaint pattern the paragraph sets up.
questions.stem: The airline’s decision to unbundle ticket prices — charging separately for baggage, seat selection, and meals — was designed to advertise a lower base fare than competitors. Consumer complaints in the following year focused overwhelmingly on _______

options.A: the airline’s base fares being too expensive.
options.B: the final cost, after add-ons, being higher than expected.
options.C: the airline’s meals being of unusually high quality.
options.D: baggage fees being eliminated entirely.

questions.explanation: Direct, foreseeable consequence of brittle, poorly-maintained pipes meeting an unusually cold winter. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the setup emphasizing vulnerability and lack of preparation.
questions.stem: Years of reduced funding for basic infrastructure maintenance left the city’s water pipes far more brittle than official records indicated. When an unusually cold winter arrived, dozens of pipes across the city _______

options.A: performed better than expected despite their age.
options.B: burst within the same forty-eight-hour period.
options.C: were replaced proactively before any damage occurred.
options.D: remained undamaged due to new insulation standards.

questions.explanation: The sentence explicitly promises “a single policy change” as the specific cause — this option names one concretely. (A), (C), and (D) are all vague, generic statements that could apply to almost any environmental program, failing to deliver the promised specific detail.
questions.stem: The city’s new composting initiative diverted an unusually large volume of waste from landfills in its first year — not through public participation alone, but because a single policy change made the real difference: _______

options.A: residents were generally supportive of environmental initiatives.
options.B: commercial restaurants, not households, were made subject to mandatory composting.
options.C: the program was well-designed and effective overall.
options.D: composting is an important part of waste management.

questions.explanation: The sentence promises “one overlooked factor” specifically — this option delivers a concrete, traceable cause. (A), (C), and (D) are vague and non-specific, failing to name the promised factor.
questions.stem: The turnaround in the struggling company’s fortunes wasn’t due to a single dramatic decision, but analysts eventually traced most of the recovery to one overlooked factor: _______

options.A: the company had simply gotten lucky with market conditions.
options.B: a renegotiated supplier contract that cut input costs by a fifth.
options.C: the leadership team worked very hard during this period.
options.D: the overall business strategy was fundamentally sound.

questions.explanation: “Sediment core samples revealed” promises a specific, evidence-based finding — a drought is a concrete, testable cause matching what sediment cores can actually reveal (climate data). (A), (C), and (D) are all vague and don’t connect to what sediment analysis would specifically show.
questions.stem: Historians long debated why the ancient city was suddenly abandoned, until sediment core samples from a nearby lakebed revealed the specific cause: _______

options.A: the city’s population had simply grown too large to sustain.
options.B: a decade-long drought had made agriculture there impossible.
options.C: the region experienced significant historical change.
options.D: ancient cities were often abandoned for various reasons.

questions.explanation: The sentence promises “one specific marketing decision” — this option names a concrete, identifiable action. (A), (C), and (D) are all generic statements that fail to specify any decision at all.
questions.stem: The film’s unexpected box-office success surprised even its own studio, which later attributed it to one specific marketing decision made almost as an afterthought: _______

options.A: the film had a talented cast and crew.
options.B: releasing a single, low-budget trailer on social media two weeks before launch.
options.C: the story resonated with audiences in general.
options.D: the studio had a strong marketing department.

questions.explanation: Delivers the promised “specific change” concretely. (A), (C), and (D) remain vague, generic explanations that don’t name any specific tactical change.
questions.stem: The team’s late-season improvement puzzled commentators until the coach revealed the specific change behind it: _______

options.A: the players had worked hard to improve as a team.
options.B: a shift from a three-defender to a four-defender formation.
options.C: the team had a new sense of belief and confidence.
options.D: the coaching staff made several small adjustments.

questions.explanation: “One decision” is delivered specifically and ties to the writing quality reviewers would credit for narrative improvement — the most plausible specific cause for improvement “in nearly every way” being tied to story. (A), (C), and (D) are specific but relate to scale/reach rather than the substantive creative improvement being described.
questions.stem: Reviewers agreed the sequel improved on the original in nearly every way, crediting the change most directly to one decision the studio made early in production: _______

options.A: hiring a much larger visual effects team.
options.B: bringing back the original screenwriter, who had been replaced for the first film.
options.C: spending significantly more on the overall production budget.
options.D: choosing to release the film in more theaters worldwide.

questions.explanation: “Specific, almost mundane cause” is delivered concretely and fits the “mundane” description well. (A), (C), and (D) are vague generalities, not a specific, identifiable cause.
questions.stem: The sudden drop in the neighborhood’s crime rate baffled residents until police data pointed to a specific, almost mundane cause: _______

options.A: the community had generally become safer over time.
options.B: the installation of brighter streetlighting along three main corridors.
options.C: crime rates fluctuate naturally from year to year.
options.D: residents had become more cautious in general.

questions.explanation: “A change nobody would have predicted” promises something specific and counter-intuitively small — this option delivers exactly that. (A), (C), and (D) are all plausible but unsurprising, generic operational improvements, contradicting “nobody would have predicted.”
questions.stem: The airline’s on-time performance improved dramatically after a change nobody outside the industry would have predicted: _______

options.A: hiring more staff across all departments.
options.B: rescheduling a single hub airport’s peak departure window by twenty minutes.
options.C: investing heavily in newer aircraft.
options.D: improving communication with passengers overall.

questions.explanation: Delivers the promised “one internal insight” specifically and concretely, matching a very common real-world pivot story. (A), (C), and (D) are all generic observations, not a specific insight “almost dismissed.”
questions.stem: The startup’s pivot from a failing consumer app to a business-to-business tool succeeded largely because of one internal insight the founders almost dismissed: _______

options.A: that businesses generally have more money to spend than consumers.
options.B: that a minor internal tool they’d built for themselves solved a widespread problem.
options.C: that the market for consumer apps was very competitive.
options.D: that pivoting is sometimes necessary for startups to survive.

questions.explanation: Names a specific translation decision, directly contrasting with “fidelity to the original text” as the sentence sets up. (A) and (D) are generic process/publishing facts, not a translation choice. (C) directly contradicts “less to fidelity.”
questions.stem: The novel’s translator later explained that the book’s success in English owed less to fidelity to the original text than to one specific choice: _______

options.A: working closely with a skilled editor throughout the process.
options.B: deliberately rewriting the protagonist’s internal monologue in a more colloquial register.
options.C: staying as faithful as possible to the source language.
options.D: publishing the book with a major international publisher.

questions.explanation: Matches the explicitly qualified finding (most improved, a subset did not). (A) and (D) overstate into universal claims the paragraph explicitly contradicts. (C) understates, ignoring the “meaningful reduction” for most participants.
questions.stem: The clinical trial showed a meaningful reduction in symptoms for most participants, though researchers were careful to note that a small subset saw no improvement at all. The overall conclusion, they emphasized, was that the treatment _______

options.A: works for absolutely everyone who takes it.
options.B: appears effective for many, though not all, patients.
options.C: has been proven to have no effect whatsoever.
options.D: should be immediately mandated for all patients with the condition.

questions.explanation: Matches “not universal” and “varying” — a nuanced, non-unanimous split, consistent with the paragraph’s qualified framing. (A) and (D) both assert unanimity, contradicting “not universal” and “varying.” (C) is unrelated and implausible for survey respondents.
questions.stem: The survey found broad, though not universal, support for the proposed reform, with opinions varying significantly by age group. Younger respondents were considerably more favorable, while older respondents remained _______

options.A: unanimously and enthusiastically supportive.
options.B: more divided, with a slight majority opposed.
options.C: completely unaware the survey existed.
options.D: unanimously opposed without exception.

questions.explanation: Matches “modest” effect and the explicit caution against overstatement. (A) and (D) overstate into revolutionary/definitive claims the paragraph explicitly warns against. (C) understates, ignoring the real, if modest, benefit found.
questions.stem: The report concluded that while the new drug reduced average recovery time, the effect size was modest and the researchers cautioned against overstating its clinical significance. Doctors, they suggested, should view it as _______

options.A: a revolutionary breakthrough that changes standard treatment entirely.
options.B: one modestly useful option among several, not a definitive solution.
options.C: something with no practical value in clinical settings.
options.D: a treatment that should replace all existing alternatives immediately.

questions.explanation: Matches “promising but far from guaranteed” precisely. (B) and (C) both assert unwarranted certainty in opposite directions. (D) contradicts analysts actively assessing risks, which implies real interest in the outcome.
questions.stem: Analysts described the merger’s prospects as promising but far from guaranteed, citing regulatory hurdles and cultural differences between the two companies as real, if not necessarily fatal, risks. Their forecast, in short, was _______

options.A: cautious optimism rather than confident certainty.
options.B: complete confidence that the merger would fail.
options.C: absolute certainty that the merger would succeed without issue.
options.D: total indifference to whether the merger happened at all.

questions.explanation: Matches “confidence in the near-term trend” specifically, while respecting the stated long-term uncertainty by not extending that confidence too far. (A) contradicts “confidence in the near-term.” (C) overextends confidence into the long term, which the paragraph explicitly separates out as uncertain. (D) contradicts “confidence” with an unsupported reversal claim.
questions.stem: The panel’s report acknowledged genuine uncertainty in long-term projections while still expressing confidence in the near-term trend, which it described as _______

options.A: completely unpredictable in every respect.
options.B: reasonably clear for the next two to three years.
options.C: certain to continue unchanged for the next fifty years.
options.D: already reversing based on preliminary, unconfirmed data.

questions.explanation: Matches the explicit “nuanced” framing — sound overall, with specific weak spots. (A) ignores the acknowledged weaknesses. (C) and (D) overstate into sweeping negative claims the paragraph explicitly contradicts by calling the overall controls “sound.”
questions.stem: The auditor’s findings were nuanced: significant weaknesses existed in three specific departments, but the organization’s overall financial controls were sound. The report’s summary line reflected this balance, describing the organization as _______

options.A: entirely free of any financial control issues.
options.B: fundamentally sound but with targeted areas needing improvement.
options.C: riddled with financial mismanagement throughout every department.
options.D: beyond any hope of meaningful reform.

questions.explanation: Matches the qualified stance — slowing decline, not guaranteeing reversal, given limited resources. (A) overstates into guaranteed revival, contradicting her explicit caution. (C) and (D) understate, contradicting her belief that decline “could be slowed.”
questions.stem: The linguist’s research suggested the endangered language’s decline could be slowed, though she stopped short of claiming it could be fully reversed given how few fluent speakers remained. Her recommendations focused on _______

options.A: guaranteeing the language’s complete revival within a decade.
options.B: realistic, incremental steps to preserve what remained.
options.C: abandoning any preservation effort as futile.
options.D: declaring the language already extinct.

questions.explanation: Matches the balanced assessment — safe now, but proactive action needed before the decade-long window closes. (A) and (D) are alarmist responses the paragraph explicitly rules out. (C) is dismissive, also explicitly ruled out.
questions.stem: The engineer’s assessment of the aging bridge was neither alarmist nor dismissive: it remained safe for current traffic loads but would require significant reinforcement within the next decade to remain so. Local officials were advised to _______

options.A: close the bridge to all traffic immediately.
options.B: begin budgeting now for reinforcement work over the coming years.
options.C: ignore the assessment entirely, since it was not urgent.
options.D: declare the bridge permanently unsafe for any use.

questions.explanation: Matches “neither full approval nor full rejection,” pointing to the specific, differentiated middle path the sentence sets up. (A) and (C) are exactly the two extremes explicitly ruled out. (D) avoids any decision, which doesn’t match a “recommending” committee.
questions.stem: The committee’s review found the proposed budget cuts were justifiable in some departments but excessive in others, recommending neither full approval nor full rejection, but rather _______

options.A: an unconditional approval of the entire budget as originally proposed.
options.B: a department-by-department revision based on the review’s specific findings.
options.C: a complete rejection of any cuts whatsoever.
options.D: an indefinite postponement of the decision entirely.

questions.explanation: Matches “likely, but not conclusively” and “fell short of definitive proof” precisely. (A) and (D) overstate into certainty the paragraph explicitly denies. (C) understates, ignoring the “likely” and “stylistic similarities” already noted.
questions.stem: The panel’s linguistic analysis found the disputed text likely, but not conclusively, written by the same author as the earlier known works, based on stylistic similarities that fell short of definitive proof. Their published finding was carefully worded to state that the attribution was _______

options.A: proven beyond any reasonable doubt.
options.B: plausible, though not fully certain.
options.C: entirely without merit or evidence.
options.D: confirmed by definitive physical evidence.

questions.explanation: Directly follows from the “selection bias” critique — the specific, logical limitation this creates for generalizability. (A) overstates into a conclusion of failure the paragraph doesn’t support. (C) is an unsupported absolute claim. (D) is an extreme, unwarranted policy recommendation.
questions.stem: Proponents of the four-day workweek point to several pilot programs showing no drop in productivity despite the reduced hours. Critics counter that these pilots were mostly conducted at companies that volunteered for the trial — firms already inclined toward flexible, well-managed work practices. This selection bias suggests that _______

options.A: the four-day workweek definitely fails in most companies.
options.B: the results may not generalize to less flexible or less well-managed organizations.
options.C: productivity is entirely unrelated to the number of hours worked.
options.D: all future pilot programs should be immediately abandoned.

questions.explanation: Precisely captures the described disagreement — both sides agree scores can be measured; they disagree about what those numbers mean. (A) misstates the dispute as being about measurement itself. (C) and (D) introduce unrelated issues not raised in the paragraph.
questions.stem: Defenders of standardized testing argue it provides an objective, comparable measure of student achievement across vastly different schools. Critics respond that “objective” scores can still reflect unequal access to test preparation resources rather than underlying ability. The disagreement, at its core, is really about _______

options.A: whether test scores can be measured accurately at all.
options.B: what the scores actually represent, not whether they can be measured.
options.C: whether schools should exist in their current form.
options.D: which specific test format is easiest to administer.

questions.explanation: Directly follows from the historical pattern of overpromising cited by opponents — reasonable skepticism, not certainty either way. (B) contradicts the cited historical underperformance. (C) contradicts the paragraph’s entire focus on cost savings as central to the debate. (D) overstates into certainty the historical pattern alone doesn’t guarantee.
questions.stem: Supporters of the merger emphasize the cost savings from combined operations, projecting significant efficiency gains within two years. Opponents point out that similar mergers in the same industry have historically underperformed their own efficiency projections by a wide margin. This history suggests that _______

options.A: the projected savings should be treated with some skepticism.
options.B: mergers always succeed regardless of industry track record.
options.C: cost savings are irrelevant to merger decisions.
options.D: this particular merger is certain to fail.

questions.explanation: Follows logically — since the curriculum targets skills (problem-solving) that standardized tests may not capture, fair evaluation needs broader measures. (A) and (C) rely solely on the measure the paragraph suggests may be incomplete for this purpose. (D) dismisses a legitimate point raised, which a “fair” evaluation wouldn’t do.
questions.stem: Advocates for the new curriculum argue that project-based learning better prepares students for real-world problem-solving than traditional lecture formats. Skeptics note that standardized test scores, the most common measure of academic achievement, have shown no significant change under the new approach. Evaluating the curriculum fairly, then, requires _______

options.A: relying exclusively on standardized test scores as the only valid measure.
options.B: considering outcomes beyond test scores that the new approach specifically targets.
options.C: abandoning the new curriculum immediately based on test results alone.
options.D: ignoring the skeptics’ concerns entirely.

questions.explanation: Directly addresses the critics’ specific objection (temporary, small-scale) by proposing exactly the kind of evidence that would resolve it. (A) and (D) dismiss the debate prematurely, contradicting the paragraph’s framing of genuine, unresolved disagreement. (C) is an extreme overreaction not warranted by a valid methodological limitation.
questions.stem: Supporters of universal basic income cite pilot studies showing recipients spent the money primarily on necessities and job training, not on reduced work effort as critics feared. Critics respond that pilot programs, being temporary and small-scale, may not predict behavior under a permanent, nationwide policy. Settling the debate conclusively would likely require _______

options.A: no further data of any kind, since the question is already settled.
options.B: evidence from a longer-term, larger-scale implementation.
options.C: abandoning pilot studies as a research method entirely.
options.D: accepting the critics’ view without any further evidence.

questions.explanation: Matches “balanced assessment” — weighing genuine, context-dependent trade-offs already outlined on both sides. (A) and (D) ignore half the trade-offs just described. (C) is a false binary the paragraph’s nuanced framing explicitly rejects.
questions.stem: Proponents of nuclear energy point to its low carbon emissions and high energy density compared to renewables requiring far more land per unit of power generated. Opponents raise concerns about long-term waste storage and the high upfront capital costs of new plants. A balanced assessment would need to weigh _______

options.A: only the emissions data, since that is the most important factor.
options.B: the specific trade-offs relevant to each region’s energy needs and constraints.
options.C: nothing, since nuclear energy is either entirely good or entirely bad.
options.D: exclusively the opinions of nuclear energy’s most vocal supporters.

questions.explanation: Directly addresses the specific equity concern raised, proposing a solution that preserves the benefits while mitigating the harm. (A) and (C) ignore or overreact to the critics’ point rather than engaging with it. (D) contradicts the paragraph’s acknowledgment that different cities have different needs.
questions.stem: Advocates for congestion pricing argue it reduces traffic and funds public transit improvements, pointing to successful implementations in several major cities. Critics counter that it disproportionately burdens lower-income commuters who have fewer alternatives to driving. Effective policy design, many suggest, would need to _______

options.A: ignore the concerns of lower-income commuters entirely.
options.B: pair congestion pricing with targeted relief for those most affected.
options.C: abandon congestion pricing as a concept altogether.
options.D: apply the exact same policy in every city regardless of local conditions.

questions.explanation: Directly follows the “not whether… but on” framing — the real, specific question the paragraph is steering toward. (A) is an extreme not indicated by the nuanced debate described. (C) and (D) introduce narrow, unrelated tangents.
questions.stem: Supporters of remote work point to studies showing improved employee satisfaction and reduced office overhead costs. Skeptics note that spontaneous, informal collaboration — often credited with sparking innovation — is harder to replicate virtually. The debate increasingly centers not on whether remote work is inherently good or bad, but on _______

options.A: whether offices should be abolished entirely and immediately.
options.B: how organizations can deliberately recreate the benefits of informal collaboration.
options.C: which specific software tool is best for video calls.
options.D: whether employees should be paid less for working remotely.

questions.explanation: Directly addresses both sides’ legitimate points — using the promising trial data while addressing the specific gap (short duration) that opponents raise. (A) and (B) are extremes that ignore one side’s legitimate concern entirely. (D) dismisses the trial evidence the paragraph treats as real and “measurable.”
questions.stem: Proponents of gene-edited crops argue they can increase yields and reduce pesticide use, citing field trials with measurable results. Opponents raise concerns about long-term ecological effects that trials, by their short duration, cannot fully capture. Reasonable policy, in this light, might favor _______

options.A: an outright, permanent ban on all gene-edited crops.
options.B: unrestricted approval with no monitoring requirements at all.
options.C: phased approval paired with long-term ecological monitoring.
options.D: ignoring the trial data entirely in favor of speculation.

questions.explanation: Draws a reasonable, evidence-based synthesis from real-world precedent, addressing the pacing concern specifically raised by opponents. (B) and (C) are absolute claims contradicting the premises already established in the paragraph. (D) is a dismissive overreach not supported by genuinely balancing both sides.
questions.stem: Supporters of the new zoning law argue it will increase housing supply and moderate rising rents over time. Opponents worry it will alter neighborhood character faster than existing communities can reasonably adapt. Cities that have implemented similar reforms elsewhere suggest that _______

options.A: both concerns can be partially addressed through phased, gradual implementation.
options.B: neighborhood character never actually changes as a result of zoning laws.
options.C: housing supply is completely unrelated to zoning regulations.
options.D: opponents of zoning reform are always factually incorrect.

questions.explanation: Directly fulfills “prove him right” — a concrete instance where human observation succeeded where automation elsewhere failed. (B) and (D) contradict “prove him right.” (C) makes his vindication pointless and contradicts the setup.
questions.stem: The old lighthouse keeper had refused every offer to automate his post, insisting that a human eye caught things sensors missed. When the storm that would prove him right finally came, _______

options.A: the automated system elsewhere failed to detect the same danger in time.
options.B: he decided automation was the better option after all.
options.C: the lighthouse was destroyed regardless of his efforts.
options.D: he retired the following week, unrelated to the storm.

questions.explanation: Follows the narrative logic directly — the specific obstacle (her father’s illness) has now been removed, making acceptance the natural next beat. (A) and (D) contradict the buildup toward this decision. (C) undercuts the entire setup of “offered a third time.”
questions.stem: She had turned down the promotion twice before, unwilling to relocate while her father was ill. When he passed and the position was offered a third time, _______

options.A: she declined once more, for entirely unrelated reasons.
options.B: she finally accepted, ready for the change she had long postponed.
options.C: the company had already filled the position with someone else.
options.D: she resigned from the company entirely.

questions.explanation: The setup (“until”) clearly signals his streak is about to be broken by this specific opponent. (A) contradicts the clear signal that this match is different. (C) and (D) sidestep the decisive outcome the “until” framing sets up.
questions.stem: The chess prodigy had never lost a match against an opponent his own age, until a quiet, unassuming twelve-year-old sat across the board from him at the regional finals. Three hours later, _______

options.A: he had extended his unbeaten streak once again, as expected.
options.B: he shook hands, having just lost his first match to a peer.
options.C: the match was declared a draw by the officials.
options.D: both players withdrew from the tournament.

questions.explanation: Matches the established pattern of resilience (“survived two economic downturns”) — the bakery’s track record suggests it would weather this threat too. (A) contradicts the resilience theme built up. (C) is an unrelated event not set up by the paragraph. (D) contradicts the bakery’s identity as being built on that specific recipe.
questions.stem: The small bakery had survived two economic downturns on the strength of a single recipe passed down for three generations. When a large chain opened directly across the street, longtime customers worried the bakery’s days were numbered. A year later, _______

options.A: the bakery had closed, unable to compete with the chain’s prices.
options.B: the bakery was thriving, its loyal customer base largely unchanged.
options.C: the large chain had also closed due to unrelated issues.
