options.D: the bakery had abandoned its original recipe entirely.

questions.explanation: Fulfills the narrative setup of an unconventional path leading to unexpected success. (A) undercuts the entire narrative arc being built. (C) and (D) are irrelevant tangents that don’t resolve the story.
questions.stem: The young violinist had been rejected by the conservatory twice, each time citing “insufficient technical polish.” Rather than reapplying a third time, she spent a year busking in the city’s subway stations instead. A talent scout who happened to pass through _______

options.A: dismissed her performance as unremarkable.
options.B: offered her a spot in a professional touring orchestra.
options.C: was actually looking for a completely different kind of musician.
options.D: had never heard of the conservatory that rejected her.

questions.explanation: Matches the setup that the case was never really “solved” — new technology naturally reveals what old methods missed. (A) contradicts the detective’s stated belief that it wasn’t truly solved. (C) and (D) sidestep the resolution the paragraph is building toward.
questions.stem: The retired detective had always maintained that one case, closed decades earlier, had never truly been solved — just abandoned. When new forensic technology reopened the file, _______

options.A: it confirmed the original, decades-old conclusion exactly.
options.B: it revealed a suspect no one had previously considered.
options.C: the case file had been lost entirely and could not be reopened.
options.D: the detective refused to look at the new evidence.

questions.explanation: Follows the natural, hopeful arc of the story — a small beginning growing into something larger. (A) and (D) contradict the constructive trajectory the story sets up. (C) is irrelevant to the village’s own outcome, which is what the sentence is tracking.
questions.stem: The remote village had no access to electricity until a group of engineering students, on a class project, installed a small solar microgrid over a single summer. Five years later, _______

options.A: the village had reverted entirely to its previous way of life.
options.B: that small grid had expanded into the region’s main power source.
options.C: the students had forgotten about the project entirely.
options.D: the village had been abandoned by its residents.

questions.explanation: The narrative setup (eleven years of nothing, framed as leading somewhere, plus the ironic “unremarkable Tuesday”) signals a payoff is coming. (B), (C), and (D) all deflate the story with anticlimax, contradicting the clear narrative buildup toward a discovery.
questions.stem: The amateur astronomer had scanned the same patch of night sky for eleven years without ever finding anything worth reporting. On what he later called an unremarkable Tuesday, _______

options.A: he finally spotted a comet that would later bear his name.
options.B: he decided to give up stargazing altogether.
options.C: his telescope broke beyond repair.
options.D: nothing unusual happened, as on every other night.

questions.explanation: A classic, well-signaled narrative turn — shared crisis prompting unlikely cooperation between rivals. (A) and (C) contradict the constructive turn the “threatened to shut down both” setup suggests is coming. (D) contradicts the stated threat to both kitchens.
questions.stem: The two rival restaurants had competed for the same customers for twenty years, each convinced the other would eventually fail. When a citywide gas shortage threatened to shut down both kitchens, _______

options.A: the owners refused to speak to each other, as always.
options.B: they pooled resources and shared a single working kitchen for weeks.
options.C: both restaurants closed permanently within the same month.
options.D: neither restaurant was affected by the shortage at all.

questions.explanation: Fulfills the narrative setup of an unexpected spark reawakening a dormant passion — a common, well-signaled emotional payoff. (A), (C), and (D) all contradict the warm, reawakening trajectory the anecdote is clearly building toward.
questions.stem: The elderly composer had not written a new piece in over a decade, convinced his best work was behind him. When his granddaughter, learning piano for the first time, played him a simple melody she had made up herself, _______

options.A: he dismissed it as childish and unremarkable.
options.B: he found himself humming it for days, and began composing again.
options.C: he decided to give up music entirely.
options.D: he was too busy to listen to her at all.

questions.explanation: Directly follows from the stated fragile assumption being violated almost immediately. (A) contradicts the model’s own stated dependency on an assumption that just failed. (C) contradicts “trade tensions escalated.” (D) is an irrelevant, nonsensical pivot.
questions.stem: The economist’s model predicted the policy would boost employment, but only under an assumption of stable global trade conditions that, in practice, rarely held for more than a year or two at a time. When trade tensions escalated shortly after implementation, _______

options.A: the policy’s effects tracked the model’s predictions closely regardless.
options.B: the real-world outcome diverged sharply from the model’s forecast.
options.C: global trade conditions became more stable than ever before.
options.D: the policy was implemented in a completely different country instead.

questions.explanation: Directly resolves the specific dilemma described (untranslatable pun) with the most creative, commonly used solution translators actually use. (A) doesn’t solve the described problem at all — it’s not really a translation “solution.” (C) is a wild overreaction to a single passage. (D) explicitly contradicts “her eventual solution,” implying she found a way to preserve rather than lose it.
questions.stem: The translator faced a specific dilemma: the original text relied on a pun with no equivalent in the target language, and any literal translation would lose the joke entirely. Her eventual solution was to _______

options.A: leave the passage completely untranslated in the final text.
options.B: invent a different pun in the target language that preserved the comic effect, if not the exact words.
options.C: remove humor from the entire book to maintain consistency.
options.D: translate the passage literally, accepting the lost joke.

questions.explanation: The clustering of supposedly rare events logically points to the underlying data/assumptions being outdated — a standard, sensible engineering conclusion (often tied to climate change, though the paragraph doesn’t need to say so explicitly). (B) dismisses a pattern the paragraph treats as significant enough to prompt a conclusion. (C) and (D) contradict the implied inadequacy suggested by the defenses being repeatedly overwhelmed.
questions.stem: The city’s flood defenses had been designed for a “hundred-year storm,” a statistical benchmark based on historical rainfall data collected decades earlier. When three such storms struck within a single decade, engineers were forced to conclude that _______

options.A: the original historical data likely no longer reflected current conditions.
options.B: the storms were simply an extraordinarily unlikely coincidence with no broader implication.
options.C: the flood defenses had performed exactly as intended.
options.D: no further investment in flood defense was necessary.

questions.explanation: Fits the described entrenched impasse — a simple fix is unlikely to be immediately embraced when the real sticking point (as with many stalled negotiations) is about principle or precedent, not just the number itself; “initially” signals this reaction may later change. (A) contradicts “initially,” which implies some resistance before eventual movement. (C) contradicts the associate’s suggestion being framed as new. (D) is an excessive overreaction to a reasonable proposal.
questions.stem: The negotiation had reached an impasse over a single number: each side’s final offer differed by less than two percent of the total contract value, yet neither would move. A junior associate suggested splitting the difference exactly in half, a proposal both sides initially _______

options.A: accepted immediately without any hesitation.
options.B: dismissed as too simple to address the real, underlying tension.
options.C: had already proposed themselves earlier in the talks.
options.D: found offensive and refused to discuss further.

questions.explanation: The discovery directly removes the estate’s core objection (not knowing her true intent) — a natural, logical consequence. (A) contradicts the significance the paragraph places on this discovery. (C) contradicts “outlining exactly how she intended to end the story.” (D) is an unsupported new claim the paragraph gives no basis for.
questions.stem: The novelist’s estate had long refused to authorize a sequel to her unfinished final manuscript, arguing any completion by another writer would betray her original vision. Decades later, the discovery of her personal notes, outlining exactly how she intended to end the story, _______

options.A: changed nothing about the estate’s position.
options.B: led the estate to finally authorize a completion based on those notes.
options.C: revealed she had never intended to finish the story at all.
options.D: was dismissed by scholars as an obvious forgery.

questions.explanation: Matches “unexpected secondary finding” precisely — an unrelated benefit is a classic, real-world pattern (drug repurposing) and fits the surprise framing. (A) isn’t really a “finding” worth highlighting as unexpected. (C) contradicts “modest effect,” which implies some improvement, not worsening. (D) doesn’t constitute a meaningful secondary finding at all.
questions.stem: The pharmaceutical trial’s most striking result wasn’t the drug’s effect on the target condition, which was modest, but an unexpected secondary finding: patients also reported _______

options.A: no side effects of any kind throughout the trial.
options.B: significant improvement in an entirely unrelated chronic condition.
options.C: a worsening of the original target condition.
options.D: complete indifference to having taken the drug at all.

questions.explanation: “However” signals a reversal of the initially feared outcome — a well-documented real-world pattern with urban park conversions (the “High Line effect”). (A) confirms rather than reverses the fear, contradicting “however.” (C) and (D) sidestep the clear contrast the sentence sets up.
questions.stem: The city’s plan to convert an abandoned rail line into a public park faced fierce initial opposition from nearby property owners concerned about foot traffic and noise. Once construction was complete, however, property values along the new park _______

options.A: fell sharply, confirming the owners’ original concerns.
options.B: rose significantly, reversing most owners’ initial opposition.
options.C: remained completely unchanged in every respect.
options.D: were never tracked or measured by any official body.

questions.explanation: “Upon closer examination” plus the emphasis on stumbling onto something during a “routine” audit signals a significant, escalating discovery, not a trivial one. (A) deflates the buildup the sentence has constructed. (C) contradicts the framing of this as a new “discrepancy” found during the audit. (D) makes no sense given it’s described as a discrepancy “in a single subsidiary’s accounts.”
questions.stem: The company’s internal audit was meant to be routine, but auditors stumbled onto a discrepancy in a single subsidiary’s accounts that, upon closer examination, _______

options.A: turned out to be a minor, easily explained clerical error.
options.B: revealed a pattern of misreporting stretching back several years.
options.C: had already been fully disclosed in previous public filings.
options.D: was unrelated to any of the subsidiary’s actual finances.

questions.explanation: “Something the team had never documented before” signals a genuinely surprising finding — a dramatic range expansion delivers on that promise specifically. (A) is exactly what was expected, contradicting “never documented before.” (C) and (D) don’t constitute a meaningful scientific finding about migration at all.
questions.stem: The marine biologists had tagged the whale to study its typical migratory route along the coast. Signal data over the following year showed something the team had never documented before: _______

options.A: the whale following the exact route previously assumed.
options.B: the whale crossing an entire ocean basin, far beyond its expected range.
options.C: the tagging device malfunctioning within the first week.
options.D: the whale remaining in the exact same location for the entire year.

questions.explanation: The setup explicitly contrasts with “territory or resources” (what was expected), so the answer must name something different and specific — a symbolic, non-material issue fits precisely and is a well-documented real pattern in actual peace negotiations. (A) and (C) directly contradict the “not about territory or resources” framing. (D) contradicts “most difficult clause,” which implies high, not low, importance.
questions.stem: The peace accord’s most difficult clause wasn’t about territory or resources, as both sides had expected going into negotiations, but about _______

options.A: territorial boundaries, which took the longest to resolve.
options.B: the wording of a formal apology, a symbolic issue neither side would compromise on.
options.C: resource-sharing agreements that were settled within the first week.
options.D: a technical matter that no one considered particularly important.

questions.explanation: Captures the paragraph’s actual point — the failure of the rationality assumption as a general finding. (A) and (B) are each just one supporting example, too narrow to represent the whole point. (D) overstates into “entirely wrong about everything,” which the paragraph never claims.
questions.stem: For decades, economists assumed rational actors would always choose the option that maximized their financial return. Behavioral economics has since shown this assumption breaks down repeatedly in practice: people routinely choose smaller, immediate rewards over larger, delayed ones, and often let emotion override calculation entirely. This isn’t a minor exception — it’s now considered central to understanding real-world economic behavior.

options.A: People often prefer smaller rewards now over larger rewards later.
options.B: Emotion frequently overrides careful financial calculation in individual decisions.
options.C: Behavioral economics has shown that the classical assumption of purely rational choice fails to explain real economic behavior.
options.D: Classical economics was entirely wrong about every aspect of human decision-making.

questions.explanation: Captures the overall claim the data point supports — the program’s connection to retention. (A) and (C) are single specific features, not the point of citing them. (D) introduces a claim about satisfaction the paragraph never actually makes.
questions.stem: The company’s new onboarding program pairs every new hire with a mentor from a different department, requires a structured thirty-day check-in schedule, and includes a formal skills assessment at the ninety-day mark. Internal data shows employees who complete the full program are significantly more likely to still be with the company after two years than those hired before the program existed.

options.A: The company assigns every new hire a mentor from a different department.
options.B: The new onboarding program appears linked to improved long-term employee retention.
options.C: Ninety-day skills assessments are the most important part of onboarding.
options.D: Employees at the company are generally satisfied with their jobs.

questions.explanation: Captures the paragraph’s full causal chain and its actual conclusion. (A) and (B) are supporting facts, not the overall point. (D) overstates with a specific, dramatic prediction the paragraph never makes.
questions.stem: Coral bleaching events, once considered rare, have become measurably more frequent over the past three decades as ocean temperatures have risen. While healthy reefs can sometimes recover from a single bleaching event, repeated events in quick succession give reefs no time to regenerate, leading to permanent degradation in an increasing number of reef systems worldwide.

options.A: Ocean temperatures have risen over the past thirty years.
options.B: A single bleaching event is not usually fatal to a coral reef.
options.C: Increasingly frequent bleaching events are causing permanent, worldwide degradation of coral reefs.
options.D: All coral reefs will be destroyed within the next decade.

questions.explanation: Captures the paragraph’s actual point — why the effort mattered, not just how long it took. (A) and (B) are process details, not the payoff being emphasized. (D) is an unsupported comparative claim the paragraph never makes.
questions.stem: The museum’s decision to digitize its entire archive took nearly six years and required scanning over two million individual documents by hand, since many were too fragile for automated scanners. The result is a searchable database that has already been used by researchers in over forty countries — far more than could have ever visited the physical archive in the same period.

options.A: The digitization project took six years to complete.
options.B: Automated scanners could not be used on many of the documents.
options.C: The digitization effort has dramatically expanded global access to the archive’s contents.
options.D: The museum’s archive is now more valuable than any other in the world.

questions.explanation: Captures the full arc — the initial concern and the actual, contrary outcome. (A) and (B) are only the setup, not the paragraph’s actual finding. (D) overstates into a citywide consensus the paragraph never claims.
questions.stem: The city’s bike-lane expansion faced significant early criticism from business owners who feared reduced parking would hurt sales. A year after completion, surveys of businesses along the new lanes found sales had, on average, increased slightly, likely due to increased foot and bike traffic in the area.

options.A: Business owners initially opposed the bike-lane expansion.
options.B: Parking availability decreased significantly along the new bike lanes.
options.C: Despite initial business concerns, the bike-lane expansion did not harm — and may have modestly helped — nearby sales.
options.D: All businesses in the city now strongly support future bike-lane expansions.

questions.explanation: Captures both parts of the finding — the general success and the specific, disproportionate exception. (A) introduces an unsupported claim about fraud never mentioned. (C) overstates “limited access” into total absence. (D) is an extreme, unsupported recommendation.
questions.stem: A recent audit of the state’s disaster relief fund found that while the vast majority of claims were processed within the mandated thirty-day window, a small subset — fewer than five percent — took over six months to resolve, disproportionately affecting rural applicants with limited access to in-person support offices.

options.A: The disaster relief fund’s audit found significant fraud in claims processing.
options.B: Most claims were processed within the required time, but a small share of rural applicants faced major delays.
options.C: Rural applicants do not have access to in-person support offices.
options.D: The disaster relief fund should be shut down immediately.

questions.explanation: Captures the full narrative — the discovery and the resulting strategic response, which is the paragraph’s real point. (A) and (B) are supporting facts that set up the point but aren’t themselves the point. (D) overstates — the paragraph describes an adaptation, not a failure.
questions.stem: The startup’s founders initially built their product for professional photographers, but usage data revealed that over sixty percent of active users were hobbyists using the tool for simple personal projects. Recognizing this mismatch, the company redesigned its pricing and onboarding specifically around this larger, previously unaddressed user base.

options.A: The product was originally designed for professional photographers.
options.B: Over sixty percent of users were hobbyists rather than professionals.
options.C: The company adapted its product strategy after discovering its actual user base differed from its intended one.
options.D: The company’s original strategy was a complete failure from the start.

questions.explanation: Captures the full scope of findings and, crucially, the “even after controlling for” point that these effects are independent of background. (A) captures only one of the listed benefits. (B) misstates the point — income was controlled for, not shown to be irrelevant to outcomes generally. (D) overstates into an absolute guarantee the study doesn’t claim.
questions.stem: Long-term studies tracking children who attended high-quality early childhood education programs show measurable benefits persisting into adulthood, including higher rates of high school graduation and lower rates of involvement with the criminal justice system, even after controlling for family income and other background factors.

options.A: High-quality early childhood education is associated with better adult graduation rates.
options.B: Family income does not affect a child’s educational outcomes.
options.C: High-quality early childhood education shows lasting positive effects on life outcomes that persist independent of family background.
options.D: Every child who attends preschool will graduate from high school.

questions.explanation: Captures the full cause-and-effect arc — early failure, response, and successful turnaround. (A) and (B) are steps within the story, not its overall point. (D) is an extreme, unsupported conclusion contradicted by the actual turnaround described.
questions.stem: The restaurant chain’s expansion into a new country initially struggled, with several locations closing within the first year due to menu items that failed to resonate with local tastes. After significant menu localization — replacing nearly forty percent of the standard offerings with region-specific dishes — the remaining locations saw a marked turnaround in performance.

options.A: Several of the chain’s locations closed within the first year of expansion.
options.B: Forty percent of the original menu items were unpopular with local customers.
options.C: Localizing the menu to fit regional tastes reversed the chain’s early struggles in the new market.
options.D: The restaurant chain should never expand into new countries again.

questions.explanation: Captures the full, specific finding — the safety benefit alongside the important qualifier that traffic wasn’t reduced. (A) is only the qualifier, not the main finding. (C) overstates into a universal policy prescription the paragraph doesn’t make. (D) introduces an unsupported claim about causes of death never mentioned.
questions.stem: Analysis of traffic accident data across several cities found that intersections redesigned with raised pedestrian crossings saw a substantial drop in pedestrian injuries, even though overall vehicle traffic volume at those intersections remained largely unchanged.

options.A: Vehicle traffic volume did not change at the redesigned intersections.
options.B: Raised pedestrian crossings appear to reduce pedestrian injuries without reducing traffic flow.
options.C: All intersections in every city should be redesigned with raised crossings.
options.D: Pedestrian injuries are the leading cause of traffic-related deaths.

questions.explanation: Correctly scopes the finding to the specific study while including the researchers’ own caveat about generalizability. (A) overstates “reduced by a third” into “eliminates all,” and ignores the explicit generalizability caution. (C) is a sweeping policy conclusion the paragraph doesn’t support. (D) overstates the caveat about “less robust” support into “no technical support of any kind.”
questions.stem: A study of one large hospital network found that switching to electronic prescribing reduced medication errors by nearly a third, primarily by eliminating errors caused by illegible handwritten prescriptions. Researchers cautioned, however, that the results might not generalize to smaller clinics with less robust technical support.

options.A: Electronic prescribing eliminates all medication errors in every healthcare setting.
options.B: Electronic prescribing reduced medication errors substantially at one hospital network, though its broader applicability remains uncertain.
options.C: Handwritten prescriptions should be banned nationwide immediately.
options.D: Smaller clinics have no technical support of any kind.

questions.explanation: Stays scoped to the specific population studied and includes the stated open question. (A) overgeneralizes from one fox population to “all urban wildlife.” (C) is an unsupported inference not stated in the paragraph. (D) misreads the finding entirely — waste schedules are an opportunity the foxes exploit, not a “threat” described in the text.
questions.stem: Researchers studying a specific population of urban foxes found they had adapted to nocturnal scavenging patterns closely tied to local restaurant waste collection schedules, timing their activity within a narrow window each night. It remains unclear whether this behavior is learned individually or passed between generations.

options.A: All urban wildlife has adapted its behavior to human schedules.
options.B: This specific fox population has adapted its activity patterns to local waste schedules, though how this behavior spreads remains unknown.
options.C: Foxes are more intelligent than previously believed.
options.D: Restaurant waste collection schedules are the primary threat to urban wildlife.

questions.explanation: Correctly scopes to one firm’s trial and reflects the explicit caveat about representativeness. (A) and (D) overgeneralize into universal prescriptions and claims. (C) overstates “decreased significantly” into total elimination.
questions.stem: A trial of a four-day workweek at one mid-sized technology firm found productivity per employee remained stable while reported burnout decreased significantly over six months. The company has not yet decided whether to make the policy permanent, and researchers noted the firm’s flexible, project-based work style may not be representative of most workplaces.

options.A: Every company should immediately switch to a four-day workweek.
options.B: One firm’s four-day workweek trial showed promising but not necessarily generalizable results.
options.C: Burnout has been eliminated entirely at the firm.
options.D: Productivity always improves when work hours are reduced.

questions.explanation: Correctly scoped to the specific city and the specific trend described. (A) generalizes beyond the one city studied. (C) and (D) both overstate a “difficulty finding” into an absolute absence.
questions.stem: A regional survey found that among small business owners in one mid-sized city, nearly seventy percent reported difficulty finding qualified staff for entry-level positions over the past year, a notably higher rate than the same survey recorded five years earlier.

options.A: Small businesses everywhere are struggling to find qualified staff.
options.B: In this city, small business owners are reporting a growing difficulty in hiring for entry-level roles compared to five years ago.
options.C: There are no qualified workers left in the region’s labor market.
options.D: Entry-level positions no longer exist in this city.

questions.explanation: Matches the paragraph’s own explicit framing — encouraging but preliminary, requiring confirmation. (A), (C), and (D) all overstate “may reduce inflammation markers” into proof, universal applicability, or cure, all explicitly contradicted by “conclusions can be drawn” not yet being possible.
questions.stem: Preliminary results from a small clinical trial suggest the experimental compound may reduce inflammation markers in patients with a specific autoimmune condition, though the trial included only forty participants and researchers emphasized that larger trials are needed before any conclusions can be drawn.

options.A: The compound has been proven to cure the autoimmune condition.
options.B: A small preliminary trial found encouraging but inconclusive results that require larger studies to confirm.
options.C: All autoimmune conditions can now be treated with this compound.
options.D: The trial’s forty participants were fully cured of their condition.

questions.explanation: Reflects both the observed improvement and the explicit causal uncertainty the economists raised. (A) overstates certainty the paragraph explicitly denies. (C) and (D) are unsupported absolutes in opposite directions.
questions.stem: An analysis of one country’s tax reform found that, in its first two years, revenue collection improved modestly among mid-sized businesses, though economists cautioned that the initial period coincided with unusually strong overall economic growth, making it difficult to isolate the reform’s specific effect.

options.A: The tax reform is definitively responsible for the entire increase in revenue.
options.B: Revenue improved after the reform, but economists caution the reform’s specific causal role is unclear amid strong overall growth.
options.C: Tax reforms never have any measurable effect on revenue.
options.D: All countries should immediately adopt this exact tax reform.

questions.explanation: Reflects the actual scope (one neighborhood’s pilot) and the officials’ specific caveat about civic engagement. (A) and (D) are unsupported, sweeping negative claims. (C) overgeneralizes the neighborhood-level result to the entire city.
questions.stem: A pilot recycling program in one neighborhood succeeded in diverting nearly half of household waste from landfills within its first year, though city officials noted the neighborhood had unusually high participation in past civic initiatives, which may have contributed to the program’s success.

options.A: Recycling programs never work in neighborhoods with low civic engagement.
options.B: This neighborhood’s pilot program was successful, though its result may be linked to the area’s unusually high civic engagement.
options.C: The entire city’s household waste has been diverted from landfills.
options.D: All future recycling programs are guaranteed to fail.

questions.explanation: Correctly captures the specific, notable comparison the paragraph highlights. (A) and (C) overgeneralize into universal claims about testing the paragraph never makes. (D) misstates “comparable rates” as “much higher.”
questions.stem: A university’s internal review of its need-based financial aid program found that recipients graduated at rates comparable to non-recipients, a notable finding given that recipients, on average, entered with somewhat lower standardized test scores than the general student population.

options.A: Standardized test scores have no relationship to graduation rates for any student.
options.B: Financial aid recipients at this university graduated at comparable rates to others despite entering with lower average test scores.
options.C: All universities should eliminate standardized testing entirely.
options.D: Financial aid recipients graduate at a much higher rate than other students.

questions.explanation: Correctly scoped to the specific finding at this firm and the specific, notable independence from attendance. (A) overgeneralizes to all remote work and all employees. (C) misreads the point — attendance was shown to be a poor predictor, not “the only factor.” (D) is an unsupported policy leap.
questions.stem: A survey of remote employees at one multinational firm found that those working across more than three time zones from their direct manager reported lower feelings of inclusion in team decisions, even when objective measures like meeting attendance were similar to their more geographically aligned colleagues.

options.A: Remote work always reduces feelings of inclusion for every employee.
options.B: At this firm, greater time-zone distance from a manager was linked to lower reported inclusion, independent of meeting attendance.
options.C: Meeting attendance is the only factor that affects employee inclusion.
options.D: This company should eliminate remote work entirely.

questions.explanation: Correctly scoped to the specific experiment and its notable finding about first-time donors. (A) and (C) overgeneralize a single experiment’s result into a universal prescription against statistics. (D) introduces an unsupported historical comparison never made in the paragraph.
questions.stem: A field experiment testing two different email subject lines for a nonprofit’s fundraising campaign found the version emphasizing a specific beneficiary’s story generated nearly twice the donation rate of a version citing broad statistics about the cause, though the effect was strongest among first-time donors specifically.

options.A: Statistics are never effective in any kind of fundraising appeal.
options.B: A story-focused subject line outperformed a statistics-focused one in this experiment, especially among first-time donors.
options.C: All nonprofits should immediately stop using statistics in their communications.
options.D: This particular email campaign raised more money than any previous campaign in the nonprofit’s history.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the paragraph’s actual finding — a weak, not absent or reversed, correlation. (A) directly reverses the point, restating the “popular belief” the paragraph explicitly contradicts. (C) overstates “weak correlation” into “no effect whatsoever.” (D) reverses the claim into an unsupported opposite extreme.
questions.stem: Contrary to popular belief, higher-priced wines do not consistently receive higher ratings from expert tasters in blind tests; several studies have found only a weak correlation between price and perceived quality once tasters cannot see the label.

options.A: Expert tasters consistently rate more expensive wines higher, confirming popular belief.
options.B: Blind taste tests show only a weak link between a wine’s price and how experts actually rate its quality.
options.C: Price has no effect whatsoever on how wine tastes.
options.D: Cheaper wines are objectively superior to expensive wines.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the nuanced finding — net job loss alongside a real, if smaller, shift toward new roles. (A) reverses the relative scale described (“significant” losses vs. “smaller” gains). (B) understates the significant job losses described. (D) overstates “significant number” into “every.”
questions.stem: The report found that while automation eliminated a significant number of manufacturing jobs over the decade, it simultaneously created a smaller but real number of new roles in machine maintenance and systems oversight — a shift in the type of work available, not simply a net loss.

options.A: Automation created far more jobs than it eliminated during the decade.
options.B: Automation had no real impact on the manufacturing job market at all.
options.C: While automation reduced manufacturing jobs overall, it also shifted some work toward new, related roles rather than eliminating labor entirely.
options.D: Automation eliminated every manufacturing job that existed before it.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the paragraph’s reframing — internal weakness as a critical, prior factor complicating the invasion-only narrative. (A) restates the very narrative the research is shown to complicate. (C) is an unsupported extreme not claimed by the paragraph. (D) directly reverses the described relationship between dysfunction and response capacity.
questions.stem: The historian’s research complicates the traditional narrative that the empire’s decline was caused primarily by external invasion; internal administrative dysfunction, her evidence suggests, had already severely weakened the empire’s capacity to respond effectively well before major invasions began.

options.A: External invasion was the sole and primary cause of the empire’s decline.
options.B: The historian’s research suggests internal dysfunction, not invasion alone, played a critical and prior role in the empire’s decline.
options.C: The empire never faced any external invasions at all.
options.D: Internal administrative dysfunction had no relationship to the empire’s ability to respond to threats.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the paragraph’s specific reframing of relative causal weight. (A) restates the assumption the new evidence is shown to challenge. (C) understates the specificity of the finding, which does identify a cause (droughts). (D) is an unsupported absolute the paragraph doesn’t claim.
questions.stem: New evidence suggests the ancient trade route’s decline was driven less by the rise of sea trade, as long assumed, and more by a series of regional droughts that made overland travel increasingly impractical for merchants.

options.A: The rise of sea trade was definitively the primary cause of the trade route’s decline.
options.B: New evidence points to regional droughts, rather than the rise of sea trade, as the more significant cause of the route’s decline.
options.C: The trade route declined due to a combination of factors that researchers cannot identify.
options.D: Sea trade never had any impact on overland trade routes throughout history.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the specific reversed direction of causality the study suggests. (A) restates the commonly assumed direction the study explicitly contradicts. (C) understates the finding — a relationship was found, just not in the commonly assumed direction. (D) overstates into a universal, deterministic claim.
questions.stem: The study did not find that social media use causes depression in teenagers; rather, it found that teenagers already experiencing depressive symptoms were more likely to increase their social media use, suggesting the relationship may run in the opposite direction from what is commonly assumed.

options.A: Social media use is the primary cause of depression among teenagers.
options.B: The study found that depressive symptoms may lead to increased social media use, rather than the reverse.
options.C: Social media use and depression have no relationship of any kind.
options.D: All teenagers who use social media frequently will become depressed.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the reveal — the true cause contradicting media coverage. (A) restates the media’s incorrect attribution as fact. (C) directly contradicts “sales had actually been stable.” (D) contradicts the specific strategic cause identified.
questions.stem: The company’s layoffs were widely attributed in media coverage to declining sales, but internal documents later showed that sales had actually been stable; the layoffs had instead been driven by a strategic decision to reallocate spending toward an unrelated, unproven new product line.

options.A: Declining sales were the true and confirmed cause of the layoffs, as media coverage suggested.
options.B: Internal documents reveal that a strategic reallocation of spending, not declining sales, actually drove the layoffs.
options.C: The company’s sales had been declining sharply for several years before the layoffs.
options.D: The layoffs had no connection to any business decision made by the company.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the paragraph’s reframing based on patent evidence. (A) restates the popular account the paragraph is shown to complicate. (C) misstates the situation — records do exist and are cited as evidence. (D) reverses “independent teams” into a false claim of collaboration.
questions.stem: Popular accounts often credit a single inventor with the breakthrough, but patent records show that at least three independent teams were working on nearly identical solutions within the same eighteen-month period, suggesting the underlying technology’s time had simply come rather than resulting from one person’s singular genius.

options.A: A single inventor was solely and uniquely responsible for the breakthrough.
options.B: Patent records suggest the breakthrough emerged from parallel, independent efforts rather than one individual’s unique genius.
options.C: No credible records exist regarding who actually invented the technology.
options.D: The three competing teams worked together collaboratively on the same solution.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the study’s actual finding, which explicitly contradicts the stated assumption. (A) restates the very assumption the study contradicts. (C) and (D) are unsupported extremes contradicting the “statistically indistinguishable” finding.
questions.stem: Contrary to the assumption that older workers are less adaptable to new technology, a workplace study found employees over fifty adopted a new software system at rates statistically indistinguishable from younger colleagues, though they were more likely to seek formal training beforehand.

options.A: Older workers adapt to new technology more slowly than younger workers, confirming common assumptions.
options.B: The study found no meaningful age-related difference in technology adoption rates, challenging a common assumption.
options.C: Only younger workers were able to successfully use the new software system.
options.D: Older workers refused to use the new technology under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the finding of “no consistent relationship,” directly addressing and complicating the stated assumption. (A) restates the assumption the finding contradicts. (C) is an unsupported policy conclusion. (D) is a specific, unsupported claim the “no consistent relationship” finding directly rules out.
questions.stem: It is often assumed that stricter environmental regulations necessarily slow economic growth, but a comparison of regions with varying regulatory strictness found no consistent relationship between regulation levels and GDP growth rates over the studied period.

options.A: Stricter environmental regulations are proven to consistently slow economic growth.
options.B: The comparison found no consistent link between regulatory strictness and GDP growth, challenging the common assumption.
options.C: All environmental regulations should be eliminated to maximize growth.
options.D: Regions with no environmental regulations grew fastest during the studied period.

questions.explanation: Accurately reflects the employees’ account, which directly contradicts the “common narrative.” (A) restates the very narrative being contradicted. (C) directly contradicts the described “aggressive and well-funded marketing campaign.” (D) contradicts “inferior to competitors.”
questions.stem: The common narrative holds that the software’s early success was due to superior engineering, but former employees describe a product that was, by most technical measures, inferior to competitors — its success, they argue, came almost entirely from an aggressive and well-funded marketing campaign.

options.A: The product’s superior engineering was the true and confirmed source of its early success.
options.B: Former employees suggest the product’s success stemmed more from marketing than from technical superiority, contradicting the common narrative.
options.C: The product had no marketing campaign of any kind.
options.D: The product was universally regarded as the best in its category on every measure.

questions.explanation: Correctly identifies what the paragraph explicitly states is the novel’s “true subject.” (A) and (B) are setting details the paragraph explicitly frames as backdrop, not the actual focus. (D) overstates into an argumentative claim the paragraph doesn’t make — the novel isn’t described as arguing anything about decline “always” destroying relationships.

Winning proposals from the most recent cycle include a new community garden and a youth sports facility.

Each image is reviewed independently by several volunteers to ensure classification accuracy.

Citizen science projects have grown increasingly common as a way to process large scientific datasets.

Which of the following best captures the passage’s central argument?

options.A: Neuroscience has definitively proven that free will does not exist.
options.B: The neuroscience findings on decision-making are less conclusive than commonly assumed, and the deeper disagreement is about what “free will” should even mean.
options.C: Compatibilism is the only philosophically defensible position on free will.
options.D: Punishment can never be morally justified under any definition of free will.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — questioning the neuroscience’s conclusiveness, then reframing the debate around competing definitions — matches this option precisely. (A) is an extreme the passage explicitly complicates (“would be a mistake… to treat this finding as more conclusive”). (C) overstates the passage’s neutral presentation of compatibilism as one option among several, not the “only defensible” one. (D) misstates the passage’s actual claim, which is conditional (“if free will requires…then”), not a blanket assertion.

questions.stem: The kitchen analogy in the second paragraph is used primarily to:

options.A: prove that neural activity has no relationship to conscious decisions.
options.B: illustrate how preparatory activity need not determine the final outcome it precedes.
options.C: argue that cooking decisions are fundamentally different from moral decisions.
options.D: show that the original experiments were poorly designed.

questions.explanation: The analogy directly follows and illustrates the point about preparation not dictating outcome — the passage’s specific counter to the “settled” reading of the experiments. (A) overstates into “no relationship,” while the passage says activity may simply reflect preparation, not zero connection. (C) and (D) are not the analogy’s stated purpose.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a strict libertarian view of free will would be most challenged by which of the following?

options.A: Evidence that brain states are shaped by prior causes within a physical universe.
options.B: Evidence that people sometimes act against their own stated preferences.
options.C: Evidence that compatibilists disagree among themselves about definitions.
options.D: Evidence that punishment can deter future crime.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states libertarian free will is “increasingly difficult to reconcile with a physical universe governed by cause and effect” — meaning evidence of brain states being causally determined directly challenges it. (B), (C), and (D) are not the specific tension the passage identifies for the libertarian position.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “incoherent” (final paragraph) most nearly means:

options.A: loud and disorganized
options.B: logically inconsistent or unable to be sustained
options.C: emotionally distressing
options.D: scientifically unproven

questions.explanation: In context (“strict moral responsibility becomes incoherent”), the word describes a logical breakdown of the concept under a certain premise, not a literal sound or emotional quality. (A) and (C) are common but wrong senses of the word outside this context. (D) confuses “incoherent” with “unverified,” which isn’t the meaning here.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author regards the debate over free will as:

options.A: fully resolved in favor of determinism.
options.B: ultimately a matter of definitional and conceptual clarity as much as empirical fact.
options.C: irrelevant to real-world questions about punishment and responsibility.
options.D: settled decisively by the compatibilist position.

questions.explanation: The passage’s closing line explicitly frames the disagreement as being “underneath… about which questions are even the right ones to be asking” — a definitional/conceptual framing. (A) and (D) both overstate resolution the passage never claims. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of the debate’s real-world stakes for punishment and responsibility.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue definitively that consciousness cannot be explained by physical science.
options.B: explain what distinguishes the “hard problem” of consciousness from the “easy” problems and why it has proven resistant to resolution.
options.C: prove that philosophical zombies actually exist.
options.D: advocate for a specific solution to the hard problem.

questions.explanation: The passage’s entire structure — defining the distinction, explaining the resistance to resolution, presenting multiple viewpoints — matches this descriptive, explanatory purpose. (A) overstates into a definitive argument the passage doesn’t make; it presents multiple views. (C) misreads the “zombie” concept, which is used as a conceivability thought experiment, not a claim of actual existence. (D) is contradicted by the passage’s balanced presentation of competing views without endorsing one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the “easy” problems of consciousness are called “easy” because:

options.A: they require no scientific expertise to solve.
options.B: we can in principle imagine what a complete mechanistic answer to them would look like.
options.C: neuroscientists have already fully solved them.
options.D: they do not involve the brain at all.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly defines “easy” in this specific, technical sense: “we can, in principle, imagine a complete answer.” (A) directly contradicts the passage’s statement that they “represent some of the most sophisticated ongoing work in neuroscience.” (C) overstates — being imaginable in principle isn’t the same as being solved. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s description of these as being about brain processing.

questions.stem: The “philosophical zombie” thought experiment is used in the passage to:

options.A: prove that consciousness does not exist.
options.B: suggest that physical processing and subjective experience may not be identical, since a being with the former but not the latter seems conceivable.
options.C: demonstrate that all animals lack consciousness.
options.D: show that neuroscience has made no progress in understanding the brain.

questions.explanation: This is precisely how the passage frames the thought experiment’s function — as a conceivability argument suggesting non-identity between processing and experience. (A) overstates the thought experiment’s actual claim, which concerns conceivability, not proof of non-existence. (C) and (D) are unrelated to the specific point the thought experiment is used to make.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the view (mentioned in paragraph 3) that the hard problem is an illusion produced by cognitive architecture?

options.A: Neuroscientists develop a complete map of every neuron involved in visual processing.
options.B: A study shows that the intuition that “something is left out” of mechanistic explanations weakens significantly as people learn more neuroscience.
options.C: A new philosopher proposes an entirely new definition of consciousness.
options.D: Behavioral evidence about animal cognition improves significantly.

questions.explanation: This option directly supports the specific claim being tested — that the intuition itself, not the underlying reality, is what’s driving perceived difficulty, and that intuition can fade with understanding. (A), (C), and (D) don’t address the specific “illusion of intuition” claim being supported.

questions.stem: As used in the final paragraph, “adjudicate” most nearly means:

options.A: to fight or argue aggressively
options.B: to settle or decide (a dispute) authoritatively
options.C: to ignore completely
options.D: to translate into another language

questions.explanation: In context (“difficult to adjudicate, rather than merely difficult to resolve”), the word clearly means to settle or decide a dispute, paired with and distinguished from “resolve.” (A), (C), and (D) are not supported by the context.

questions.stem: The passage’s central purpose is to:

options.A: argue that legal systems should never consider outcomes when assigning punishment.
options.B: present the puzzle of moral luck and the tension it creates between two persistent, competing moral intuitions.
options.C: prove that constitutive luck makes all moral judgment meaningless.
options.D: advocate for treating both distracted drivers with identical leniency.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — introducing the phenomenon, showing the tension between control-based and outcome-based intuitions, presenting unresolved responses — matches this framing. (A) and (D) overstate into specific advocacy positions the passage explicitly declines to fully endorse (“no fully satisfying resolution… has emerged”). (C) overstates the passage’s presentation of constitutive luck as “unsettling,” not as proof that all judgment is meaningless.

questions.stem: According to the passage, “circumstantial luck” refers to:

options.A: the outcome of an action being determined by chance after a choice is made.
options.B: the fact that a person’s life circumstances may never test them the way another person’s circumstances do.
options.C: the genetic basis of a person’s temperament.
options.D: the legal system’s tendency to be inconsistent.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit definition and example (a comfortably raised person never facing the pressures another person faced). (A) describes outcome luck, a different category defined earlier. (C) describes constitutive luck, a distinct third category. (D) is not a category the passage defines at all.

questions.stem: The two drivers example is used in the passage primarily to:

options.A: prove that all traffic laws are unjust.
options.B: illustrate how identical choices can lead to very different moral judgments based purely on chance outcomes.
options.C: show that phone use while driving should be legal.
options.D: demonstrate that only intentions, never outcomes, should matter morally.

questions.explanation: This is exactly the example’s stated function — illustrating the disconnect between identical choices and different outcome-based judgments. (A) and (C) are claims never made by the passage. (D) actually states the opposite of what the passage argues is our persistent intuition (that outcomes do seem to matter to us).

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author views the “bite the bullet” response (final paragraph) as:

options.A: fully correct and the only reasonable position.
options.B: a coherent position, but one that may ask more of ordinary moral psychology than is realistic or perhaps desirable.
options.C: logically incoherent and self-contradictory.
options.D: irrelevant to the discussion of moral luck.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly presents the counter-response as noting this position “asks too much of moral psychology,” implying the author sees a real, unresolved tension rather than a clean victory for either side. (A) overstates the passage’s neutral, unresolved framing. (C) is not supported — the position is presented as coherent, just contested. (D) directly contradicts its central role in the passage’s final paragraph.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “bites the bullet” most nearly means:

options.A: refuses to engage with a difficult topic.
options.B: accepts an uncomfortable but logically consistent conclusion, despite its unpleasant implications.
options.C: offers a compromise between two extreme positions.
options.D: misunderstands the nature of the original question.

questions.explanation: This is the standard idiomatic meaning, matched by context — the response that “insists” on the strict, uncomfortable, logically consistent conclusion about responsibility. (A), (C), and (D) don’t match the context of a response that directly engages and commits to a specific, difficult position.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that nudge policies should be banned as manipulative.
options.B: explain the behavioral economics findings behind nudge policy, and present both its philosophical justification and the concerns raised against it.
options.C: prove that classical economic theory has been completely discredited.
options.D: argue that opt-out retirement schemes are the only effective policy tool available to governments.

questions.explanation: The passage’s balanced structure — findings, the nudge response, philosophical objections, and empirical caveats — matches this descriptive, multi-sided purpose. (A) overstates into advocacy the passage never takes. (C) overstates “fails in specific, predictable ways” into total discrediting of the whole framework. (D) is an unsupported exclusivity claim never made.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the opt-out retirement scheme example illustrates:

options.A: a case where individual choice is eliminated entirely.
options.B: how changing a default option can shift outcomes without changing the actual menu of choices available.
options.C: why loss aversion has no practical policy applications.
options.D: a failed nudge policy that did not increase participation.

questions.explanation: This is exactly how the passage frames the example — “the actual menu of choices… remains exactly the same,” with only the default changed. (A) directly contradicts “no one is forced to save.” (C) contradicts the entire premise of the example illustrating a practical application. (D) directly contradicts “dramatically increase participation rates.”

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward nudge policy throughout the passage can best be described as:

options.A: uncritically enthusiastic
options.B: dismissively hostile
options.C: measured, acknowledging both its rationale and legitimate concerns about it
options.D: entirely indifferent to the topic

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly presents the rationale (paragraph 3), the critics’ concerns (paragraph 3), and empirical caveats (paragraph 4) without dismissing any side outright. (A) and (B) both overstate into one-sided positions the balanced structure contradicts. (D) contradicts the passage’s clear, substantive engagement with the topic throughout.

questions.stem: The “decline effect” is mentioned in the passage primarily to:

options.A: prove that nudges never work under any circumstances.
options.B: caution that some early, striking nudge results may not hold up as reliably at larger scale.
options.C: argue that all social science research is fundamentally unreliable.
options.D: show that the retirement-savings finding has been discredited.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s specific, hedged framing — a caution about some results, not a blanket dismissal. (A) and (C) both overstate into absolutes the passage explicitly avoids (“this does not mean nudges don’t work”). (D) directly contradicts the passage’s statement that this specific finding “has proven remarkably robust.”

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “canonical” (paragraph 2) most nearly means:

options.A: religious or sacred
options.B: widely recognized as the standard or representative example
options.C: recently discovered and untested
options.D: legally mandated

questions.explanation: In context (“the canonical example is retirement savings”), the word describes a standard, most-cited representative case. (A) is a different, unrelated sense of the word. (C) directly contradicts the description of an established, repeatedly-shown effect. (D) is unsupported by context.

questions.stem: The passage’s central argument is that:

options.A: meritocracy should be immediately replaced by a hereditary system.
options.B: both the practical implementation and the philosophical premises of meritocracy face serious, unresolved challenges.
options.C: intelligence and effort have no relationship to individual success.
options.D: all wealthy countries have achieved perfect intergenerational income mobility.

questions.explanation: The passage’s two-part structure — an “empirical challenge” and a “philosophical challenge,” both explicitly named — matches this framing precisely. (A) is directly contradicted by “none of this establishes that meritocratic ideals should be abandoned outright.” (C) overstates the passage’s point, which is about the origins of these traits, not their relevance to outcomes. (D) is the opposite of what the passage’s cited studies find.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the philosophical challenge to meritocracy is distinct from the empirical challenge in that it:

options.A: focuses on unequal access to education and resources.
options.B: questions whether even meritocracy’s ideal form rests on a coherent notion of “earned” reward.
options.C: argues that intergenerational income mobility studies are methodologically flawed.
options.D: focuses exclusively on aristocratic societies of the past.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states this challenge applies “even setting aside unequal access entirely” — targeting the ideal form itself, not implementation. (A) describes the empirical challenge, explicitly distinguished from this one. (C) is not a claim the passage makes about the studies. (D) is not the philosophical challenge’s actual focus, which is about individuals’ traits, not historical systems.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that intergenerational income mobility studies are cited primarily to:

options.A: prove meritocracy has been entirely eliminated in modern societies.
options.B: support the claim that formally open systems still substantially reproduce existing family-based hierarchies.
options.C: show that talent has no influence on income at all.
options.D: demonstrate that hereditary aristocracies had higher mobility than modern meritocracies.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit use of the studies to support “persistent correlations between parental and child income” despite formal openness. (A) overstates — the passage argues reproduction persists, not that meritocracy has vanished. (C) overstates into an absolute the passage doesn’t claim. (D) is a comparison never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The author’s tone in the final paragraph can best be described as:

options.A: dismissive of any concerns about meritocracy
options.B: cautionary, urging a more nuanced view rather than treating meritocracy as an unqualified good
options.C: enthusiastically supportive of unrestrained meritocracy
options.D: entirely neutral, offering no evaluative perspective at all

questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly says the finding “should give pause to anyone tempted to treat ‘meritocracy’ as a simple, unqualified good” — a clearly cautionary stance. (A) and (C) contradict this explicit caution. (D) contradicts the clearly evaluative language used throughout (“should give pause,” “real social harm”).

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “cultural capital” most nearly refers to:

options.A: money inherited directly from one’s parents.
options.B: non-monetary social and cultural advantages, such as networks and know-how, that aid success.
options.C: government funding for arts and culture programs.
options.D: formal educational credentials only.

questions.explanation: The term is introduced alongside “education” and “networks” as part of a broader category of advantages beyond direct financial inheritance. (A) narrows the term to money alone, contradicting its listing alongside non-monetary items. (C) is an unrelated meaning not used here. (D) narrows the term too specifically to formal credentials, when the passage’s usage is broader (including “modeling of what an ambitious life trajectory looks like”).

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that the current wave of automation will definitely cause permanent mass unemployment.
options.B: examine the historical pattern of technological displacement and adaptation, and assess whether the current wave of automation genuinely breaks from that pattern.
options.C: prove that ATMs caused a permanent decline in banking employment.
options.D: advocate for a total ban on machine learning technologies in the workplace.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — establishing the historical pattern, examining the current wave’s potential difference, and reframing the debate around transition management — matches this analytical purpose. (A) is directly contradicted by the passage’s statement that even concerned observers “tend to stop short of predicting mass, permanent unemployment.” (C) directly contradicts “their numbers, initially, actually grew.” (D) is a policy position never suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the ATM/bank teller example illustrates:

options.A: a case where technology eliminated an entire profession outright.
options.B: the pattern of task displacement followed by adaptation into a new, related role.
options.C: why automation always increases unemployment in the short term.
options.D: the unique unpredictability of the current wave of automation.

questions.explanation: This is exactly how the passage frames the example, including the specific detail about tellers shifting to advisory tasks. (A) directly contradicts “their numbers, initially, actually grew.” (C) is not supported by an example the passage uses to show adaptation, not increased unemployment. (D) misapplies an example about a past wave to a claim about the “current” wave, which the passage discusses separately.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the passage’s argument that the current automation wave may differ from previous ones?

options.A: Machine learning systems have become significantly better at drafting written documents and analyzing complex data than they were a decade ago.
options.B: A new law requires all displaced workers to receive severance pay.
options.C: The overall unemployment rate has remained stable for the past five years.
options.D: A study finds that most companies still primarily use automation for repetitive manual tasks.

questions.explanation: This directly supports the passage’s specific claim that current automation is reaching into cognitive/creative domains previously considered safe, expanding the boundary described in paragraph 2. (B) and (C) are unrelated to the specific “different in kind” claim being tested. (D) would actually undercut, not support, the claim that this wave differs by reaching into cognitive work.

questions.stem: The passage’s discussion of “distributional character” (final paragraph) refers primarily to:

options.A: how technology companies distribute their profits among shareholders.
options.B: the fact that the workers displaced by automation are often not the same workers who benefit from newly created roles.
options.C: the geographic spread of internet access across different countries.
options.D: how automated systems distribute tasks among different machines.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly defines this in context — displaced and benefiting workers requiring “different skills, often concentrated in different geographic regions.” (A), (C), and (D) are all unrelated meanings not supported by the passage’s specific usage.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author believes policy discussions about automation should:

options.A: focus primarily on banning automating technologies outright.
options.B: shift emphasis toward managing the transition for workers on the losing side, rather than only debating aggregate employment effects.
options.C: ignore the transition entirely and trust that markets will resolve all problems automatically.
options.D: focus exclusively on retraining truck drivers specifically.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit closing statement about debates “shifting… toward the more tractable and arguably more urgent question of how to manage the transition.” (A) is never suggested anywhere in the passage. (C) contradicts the passage’s clear concern about uneven distribution needing active attention. (D) overly narrows a general point to one example used only for illustration.

questions.stem: The passage’s central purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all advertising-funded platforms are deliberately, consciously manipulative.
options.B: explain the structural incentives of attention-based business models and present the genuine tension between critiques and defenses of that model.
options.C: prove that users are entirely powerless against platform design.
options.D: advocate for banning digital advertising entirely.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — explaining incentives, then presenting both a critique and a defense, then acknowledging genuine tension — matches this balanced, explanatory purpose. (A) is explicitly contradicted by “does not require any single feature to be deliberately, consciously ‘addictive.’” (C) is directly contradicted by the passage’s explicit statement that “users are not, in fact, powerless.” (D) is a policy position never suggested in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why might the “market” fail to correct for the costs of attention capture?

options.A: Because users are legally prohibited from switching platforms.
options.B: Because the costs to users are diffuse and delayed, unlike a typical dissatisfaction with a physical product.
options.C: Because advertisers refuse to pay for any platform.
options.D: Because platforms do not track any user engagement data.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the “structural problem” the passage identifies — the disconnect between diffuse, delayed costs and typical, quicker market feedback. (A) and (C) are claims never made in the passage. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s discussion of “engagement metrics” being actively tracked and optimized against.

questions.stem: The phrase “revealed preference” (final paragraph) is used in the passage to refer to:

options.A: preferences people explicitly state when surveyed about their values.
options.B: what people’s actual, repeated choices over time suggest about what they value, regardless of stated preferences.
options.C: preferences that are illegal to act upon.
options.D: preferences that platforms actively conceal from users.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly defines this as “what people actually choose to spend time on, repeatedly, over years,” distinguished from what “users say, when surveyed” — i.e., distinct from stated preference. (A) directly describes the opposite concept (stated preference), which the passage distinguishes from revealed preference. (C) and (D) are unsupported, unrelated claims.

questions.stem: The author’s stance on the debate presented in the passage can best be described as:

options.A: firmly siding with the critics of attention-based business models.
options.B: firmly siding with the defenders of attention-based business models.
options.C: presenting genuine merit on both sides while highlighting an unresolved tension between them.
options.D: entirely dismissive of the entire debate as unimportant.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly calls for taking “both halves of this picture seriously at once” and names the unresolved question directly. (A) and (B) both overstate into one-sided advocacy the passage’s balanced structure doesn’t support. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s substantial, serious engagement with the topic throughout.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “paternalism” most nearly means:

options.A: a father’s specific role within a family structure.
options.B: the practice of substituting others’ judgment about what is good for them in place of their own choices.
options.C: a legal system based on inherited titles.
options.D: a business model based on advertising revenue.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit context — “substituting the critic’s judgment about what people should want for what people… actually do want.” (A) and (C) are unrelated, literal or unrelated senses of the word. (D) confuses the term with the passage’s separate topic (the business model itself).

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: prove that microfinance is a complete failure that should be abandoned.
options.B: trace how rigorous evaluation of microfinance revealed a more modest reality than its early, utopian reputation suggested, while drawing broader lessons about development interventions.
options.C: argue that all development interventions are oversold and worthless.
options.D: advocate for banning group lending models specifically.

questions.explanation: The passage’s arc — from early utopian rhetoric, through rigorous evaluation findings, to broader lessons and a specific complication — matches this analytical purpose. (A) is explicitly contradicted by “the lesson… is not that microfinance is worthless.” (C) overgeneralizes a specific, well-documented case into a sweeping claim about all interventions the passage doesn’t make. (D) is a specific policy stance never suggested in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, randomized controlled trials of microfinance found:

options.A: no effects of any kind from access to microloans.
options.B: measurable but modest effects, generally falling short of the dramatic poverty reduction originally promised.
options.C: that microfinance caused widespread economic collapse in every country studied.
options.D: that microloans were used exclusively to start new, ambitious businesses.

questions.explanation: This directly matches the passage’s specific findings — “measurable effects” alongside “little to no evidence” of the dramatic, broader claims. (A) directly contradicts “did produce measurable effects.” (C) is an extreme claim never made anywhere in the passage. (D) directly contradicts “many borrowers used loans not to start ambitious new ventures but to smooth consumption.”

questions.stem: The passage mentions microfinance’s high early visibility (paragraph 3) primarily to explain:

options.A: why microfinance is more profitable than other development interventions.
options.B: why microfinance has been unusually well studied compared to other, similarly confident development interventions.
options.C: why microfinance institutions charge higher interest rates than banks.
options.D: why microfinance was invented in the first place.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the stated reason — visibility attracted “an unusually large volume of serious academic scrutiny” other interventions lacked. (A), (C), and (D) are all claims not supported by this specific point in the passage.

questions.stem: The over-indebtedness complication described in the final paragraph is best characterized in the passage as:

options.A: proof that microfinance institutions always intend to harm borrowers.
options.B: an unintended, harmful outcome that can emerge from rapid expansion without sufficient regulatory safeguards.
options.C: evidence that group lending never works under any circumstances.
options.D: unrelated to the broader lessons the passage draws about development interventions.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit framing — “despite microfinance’s founding intentions being close to the opposite” and tied directly to “limited regulatory oversight.” (A) directly contradicts the stated benign founding intentions. (C) overstates a specific complication into a blanket condemnation of the entire model. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that this “illustrate[s] a pattern worth remembering” broadly.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “recalibration” (paragraph 3) most nearly means:

options.A: a complete and total abandonment of a prior approach
options.B: an adjustment or fine-tuning of expectations or methods based on new evidence
options.C: a financial audit of an organization’s accounts
options.D: a legal dispute between two parties

questions.explanation: In context (“a useful, broader recalibration in how development interventions are evaluated”), the word describes an adjustment in evaluative approach, not a total abandonment. (A) overstates the word’s meaning into something far more drastic than “adjustment.” (C) and (D) are unrelated senses not supported by the context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: prove definitively that language models genuinely understand language exactly as humans do.
options.B: present the debate over whether language models “understand” language, and suggest a more precise, componential way of framing the question.
options.C: argue that the Chinese Room thought experiment has been thoroughly debunked by modern AI.
options.D: advocate for banning the development of large language models.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — presenting both sides, then proposing a more granular reframing in the final paragraph — matches this analytical purpose. (A) overstates into a definitive proof the passage never makes; it presents an open debate. (C) misreads the passage, which uses the thought experiment as a live, unresolved argument, not something “debunked.” (D) is a policy position never suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The Chinese Room thought experiment is used in the passage to:

options.A: prove that all computer systems are incapable of any useful function.
options.B: illustrate the skeptics’ argument that sophisticated symbol manipulation is not the same as genuine understanding.
options.C: show that Chinese is a uniquely difficult language for computers to process.
options.D: demonstrate that language models cannot produce fluent responses.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the stated function of the thought experiment as presented by “skeptics of the ‘understanding’ framing.” (A) and (D) are extreme claims never made or contradicted by the passage’s description of fluent output. (C) misreads the thought experiment’s purpose, which is about symbol manipulation generally, not Chinese specifically.

questions.stem: According to the passage, defenders of a more expansive view of AI “understanding” argue that:

options.A: human cognition may itself be describable in similarly mechanistic terms without most people concluding human understanding is illusory.
options.B: the Chinese Room thought experiment proves language models are conscious.
options.C: understanding is a single, unified capacity that either exists fully or not at all.
options.D: language models have direct, unmediated access to the true meaning of words.

questions.explanation: This is the specific rejoinder attributed to defenders in paragraph 3.
