(B) overstates a claim never made — the passage doesn’t discuss consciousness via this thought experiment. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s final paragraph, which argues understanding is likely a cluster of separable capacities, not this claim. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s point that human cognition lacks such direct access either.

questions.stem: The final paragraph’s proposed reframing suggests that the question “does this system understand?” should be replaced with:

options.A: a question about whether the system is legally a person.
options.B: a more precise inquiry into which specific components of understanding a system does or doesn’t reliably exhibit.
options.C: a question about how much electricity the system consumes.
options.D: a question about whether the system was trained on copyrighted material.

questions.explanation: This is exactly the passage’s stated proposal — asking “which specific components of understanding a given system does and doesn’t reliably exhibit, and in which specific contexts.” (A), (C), and (D) are all unrelated questions never proposed in the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “rejoinder” most nearly means:

options.A: an unrelated new topic introduced into a conversation.
options.B: a response or reply, especially one offered in argument or rebuttal.
options.C: a formal legal document.
options.D: an apology for a previous mistake.

questions.explanation: In context (“defenders… raise a pointed rejoinder”), the word clearly refers to a rebuttal-style response within the ongoing debate. (A), (C), and (D) are unrelated or incorrect senses not supported by the context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all forms of gene editing should be permanently banned worldwide.
options.B: explain the therapeutic potential of gene editing while examining the distinct and escalating ethical questions it raises, particularly around germline editing.
options.C: prove that the 2018 controversy was based on a scientifically unsound technique.
options.D: advocate specifically for allowing genetic enhancement for cognitive traits.

questions.explanation: The passage’s arc — therapeutic potential, the somatic/germline distinction, the 2018 controversy, and the harder enhancement question ahead — matches this comprehensive, analytical purpose. (A) is contradicted by the passage’s substantial discussion of legitimate therapeutic uses. (C) directly contradicts “not primarily because the underlying editing technique was scientifically unsound.” (D) is a specific advocacy position never taken; the passage presents this as an open, difficult question.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the key distinction between somatic and germline editing is that:

options.A: somatic editing is illegal everywhere, while germline editing is legal everywhere.
options.B: germline changes are inherited by future generations, while somatic changes affect only the treated individual.
options.C: somatic editing is a newer technique than germline editing.
options.D: germline editing has never been successfully performed on any organism.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit definition of the distinction. (A) directly contradicts the passage, which never states this legal claim and instead discusses ongoing regulatory efforts. (C) is an unsupported claim about relative novelty never made. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s account of the 2018 case, where germline editing was performed on human embryos.

questions.stem: The 2018 controversy is presented in the passage primarily as an example of:

options.A: a case where the scientific community praised a scientist for pioneering breakthrough work.
options.B: a case where bypassing ethical review and societal deliberation, not the science itself, drove near-universal condemnation.
options.C: proof that gene editing technology does not actually work as intended.
options.D: an example of legitimate, well-regulated germline editing.

questions.explanation: This is exactly how the passage frames the reason for condemnation — process, not the underlying science. (A) directly contradicts “near-universal condemnation.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s statement that the technique itself was not scientifically unsound. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s description of the intervention as having “bypassed” required review processes.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author views the disease/enhancement distinction as:

options.A: a clear, easily maintained line that raises no further difficulty.
options.B: potentially difficult to maintain with philosophical rigor, given that many traits exist on a spectrum.
options.C: entirely irrelevant to future ethical debates about gene editing.
options.D: already fully resolved by current international regulations.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states geneticists’ concern that the distinction “will prove difficult to maintain with any philosophical rigor… since many traits exist on a continuous spectrum.” (A) directly contradicts this stated difficulty. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s extensive discussion of this exact distinction as a looming, urgent issue. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s framing of this as a question “looming on the horizon” that “the current moratorium does not resolve.”

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “moratorium” most nearly means:

options.A: a permanent, irreversible ban with no possibility of future change.
options.B: a temporary prohibition or suspension of an activity.
options.C: a formal scientific award or honor.
options.D: a type of gene-editing technique.

questions.explanation: The context (“the current moratorium does not resolve” a question about the technology’s future once safety improves) implies a temporary, not permanent, suspension pending further development. (A) overstates the term’s meaning into permanence, contradicted by the passage’s discussion of the issue evolving as technology “continues to improve.” (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported meanings.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: advocate strongly for the immediate global deployment of solar radiation management.
options.B: explain the appeal of geoengineering while examining the serious technical, moral, and institutional risks it poses.
options.C: prove that volcanic eruptions are the primary cause of long-term climate change.
options.D: argue that emissions reduction efforts should be entirely abandoned in favor of geoengineering.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — presenting the appeal, then substantial risks (regional harm, termination shock, governance gaps) — matches this balanced, analytical purpose. (A) is contradicted by the passage’s extensive, serious treatment of risks that goes well beyond simple advocacy. (C) misreads the volcanic reference, used only as an analogy for the cooling mechanism, not a causal claim about long-term climate change. (D) is never suggested; the passage discusses geoengineering as a response to the pace gap, not a replacement for emissions reduction.

questions.stem: According to the passage, “termination shock” refers to:

options.A: the immediate cooling effect produced when solar radiation management begins.
options.B: the rapid reassertion of full warming if a solar radiation management program is abruptly halted.
options.C: a sudden, unexpected increase in global emissions.
options.D: the political conflict caused by disagreements over climate policy.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit definition of the term. (A) describes the opposite effect — this term concerns halting, not beginning, the program. (C) and (D) are unrelated concepts not defined this way anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that solar radiation management differs from emissions reduction in which specific way?

options.A: Emissions reduction is significantly more expensive to implement in every case.
options.B: Solar radiation management could redistribute climate harms unevenly across regions, unlike emissions reduction.
options.C: Emissions reduction produces effects within months, while solar radiation management takes decades.
options.D: Solar radiation management has no associated risks of any kind.

questions.explanation: This is explicitly stated: emissions reduction “does not by its nature redistribute climate harms from one region onto another,” unlike solar radiation management. (A) reverses the passage’s actual claim about relative cost-effectiveness. (C) directly reverses the passage’s stated timelines (months for SRM, decades for emissions reduction to show comparable effect). (D) directly contradicts the passage’s extensive discussion of serious risks.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward geoengineering, as conveyed in the passage, can best be described as:

options.A: uncritically supportive
options.B: seriously engaged with both its practical appeal and its severe, largely unresolved risks
options.C: completely dismissive of the technology’s potential value
options.D: entirely neutral, with no discernible perspective offered

questions.explanation: The passage substantively engages with both the appeal (speed, cost) and severe risks (regional harm, termination shock, governance gaps) without resolving into simple advocacy or dismissal. (A) and (C) both overstate into one-sided positions the passage’s balanced treatment doesn’t support. (D) contradicts the passage’s clearly evaluative language throughout (“severe enough,” “deepest concern,” “moral and geopolitical hazard”).

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “hazard” (paragraph 3) most nearly means:

options.A: a game of chance played with dice.
options.B: a source of danger or risk.
options.C: a legal contract between two parties.
options.D: a type of atmospheric particle.

questions.explanation: In context (“a moral and geopolitical hazard distinct from anything posed by emissions reduction”), the word clearly refers to a source of danger or risk. (A) is an unrelated, archaic meaning. (C) and (D) are unrelated senses not supported by the context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: prove that quantum computers will never have any practical use.
options.B: clarify a common misconception about how quantum computing works, and outline both its realistic scope of advantage and its remaining engineering challenges.
options.C: argue that classical computers are superior to quantum computers in every respect.
options.D: explain, in full technical detail, how to build a working quantum computer.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — correcting the “trying all answers simultaneously” misconception, narrowing the realistic scope of advantage, and detailing engineering challenges — matches this clarifying, analytical purpose. (A) is contradicted by the passage’s discussion of “genuine, well-established promise” for specific problem classes. (C) overstates a comparison the passage doesn’t make in these absolute terms — quantum computers are described as advantageous for specific tasks, not universally superior or inferior. (D) misreads the passage’s level and purpose, which is conceptual and evaluative, not a technical build guide.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is the “trying all possible answers simultaneously” description misleading?

options.A: Because qubits cannot actually be placed into superposition at all.
options.B: Because measurement collapses superposition into a single random outcome, and the real source of advantage lies in interference effects that amplify correct answers before measurement.
options.C: Because classical computers can also achieve the same effect using standard bits.
options.D: Because quantum computers do not use qubits at all.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s stated correction, distinguishing mere superposition from the actual mechanism (interference) that produces useful results. (A) and (D) directly contradict the passage’s own description of qubits and superposition as real phenomena. (C) is an unsupported claim never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that quantum computers are expected to offer a meaningful advantage over classical computers primarily for:

options.A: all everyday computing tasks, including word processing and video streaming.
options.B: a narrower set of problems, including certain cryptographic and chemical simulation tasks, with a specific mathematical structure.
options.C: no computational tasks whatsoever, according to current theoretical understanding.
options.D: exclusively tasks related to video game graphics rendering.

questions.explanation: This directly matches the passage’s specific, explicit list of promising problem categories. (A) is directly contradicted by “no quantum algorithm currently known offers any meaningful advantage” for such everyday tasks. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of “genuine, well-established promise” for specific problems. (D) is a claim never made anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “decoherence” refers to:

options.A: the process by which a classical bit is set to either 0 or 1.
options.B: the loss of a qubit’s delicate quantum properties due to unwanted interaction with its environment.
options.C: a type of quantum algorithm used for cryptography.
options.D: the deliberate cooling of a quantum computer’s hardware.

questions.explanation: This is the passage’s explicit definition of the term. (A) describes a classical, not quantum, process, unrelated to this term. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported meanings not given by the passage’s usage.

questions.stem: The author’s overall tone toward claims about quantum computing’s near-term potential can best be described as:

options.A: uncritically enthusiastic, endorsing all optimistic industry projections.
options.B: measured and clarifying, correcting popular misconceptions while acknowledging genuine, if narrower, promise alongside real open challenges.
options.C: entirely dismissive, treating quantum computing as a field with no real scientific merit.
options.D: angry and hostile toward researchers working in the field.

questions.explanation: The passage carefully distinguishes real promise from popular overstatement and explicitly leaves the field’s near-term trajectory as “one of the genuinely open empirical questions.” (A) is contradicted by the passage’s explicit correction of “popular coverage” overstatement. (C) is contradicted by the passage’s substantial, respectful discussion of genuine scientific promise. (D) is an unsupported, uncharacteristic tone not reflected anywhere in the passage’s measured language.

questions.stem: The passage’s central argument is that:

options.A: human memory functions like an accurate video recording that never changes once formed.
options.B: memory is a reconstructive process vulnerable to alteration each time it is recalled, with significant practical consequences, particularly for legal testimony.
options.C: false memories can never be distinguished from real ones by any means whatsoever.
options.D: eyewitness testimony should never be used as evidence under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: The passage’s arc — overturning the storage metaphor, presenting reconstructive evidence, explaining the mechanism, and tracing legal implications — matches this comprehensive argument. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s central thesis, which explicitly overturns this “storage metaphor.” (C) overstates the passage’s actual, more nuanced claim about subjective indistinguishability from the rememberer’s own perspective, not an absolute claim about all possible means of distinguishing them. (D) is a specific policy conclusion never stated; the passage discusses reforms to how testimony is weighed, not its total exclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, “reconsolidation” refers to:

options.A: the initial encoding of a new memory at the moment an event occurs.
options.B: the process by which a retrieved memory becomes temporarily modifiable before being re-stored.
options.C: a technique used by police to deliberately implant false memories.
options.D: the permanent, complete erasure of an old memory.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s stated definition. (A) describes original encoding, explicitly distinguished from reconsolidation in the passage. (C) misreads the term as a deliberate technique rather than a natural cognitive process. (D) is an unsupported and inaccurate characterization — the passage describes modification and re-storage, not erasure.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the reconstructive nature of memory might be evolutionarily advantageous because:

options.A: it allows memories to remain perfectly unchanged over a lifetime.
options.B: it allows a memory system to incorporate newly learned, contextually relevant information over time.
options.C: it prevents any new information from ever being learned.
options.D: it eliminates the need for memory altogether.

questions.explanation: This matches the passage’s explicit “plausible trade-off” framing — updating with “new, contextually relevant information” as a practical benefit. (A) directly contradicts the reconstructive thesis the entire passage argues for. (C) and (D) are extreme, unsupported claims contradicted by the passage’s actual, more measured framing.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the passage’s discussion of eyewitness testimony reform?

options.A: A study finds that witnesses who express high confidence in their testimony are, on average, no more accurate than those expressing low confidence.
options.B: A study finds that all eyewitnesses are always completely accurate in every case.
options.C: A study finds that memory reconsolidation does not occur in any human beings.
options.D: A study finds that police interviews have no influence on witness recall whatsoever.

questions.explanation: This directly supports the passage’s specific claim that confidence “bears no reliable relationship to the memory’s actual accuracy.” (B) directly contradicts the passage’s entire thesis about memory’s fallibility. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s central mechanism explaining the phenomenon. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of misleading information (including question wording) shaping recall.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “labile” most nearly means:

options.A: permanently fixed and unchangeable.
options.B: prone to change or alteration; unstable.
options.C: related to laboratory scientific equipment.
options.D: emotionally distressing.

questions.explanation: In context (“neural circuits… become temporarily labile — open to modification”), the passage itself glosses the word as meaning open to modification. (A) is the direct opposite of the intended meaning. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported senses of the word.

questions.stem: The passage’s central argument is that:

options.A: colonial trade was entirely coercive with absolutely no economic agency exercised by colonized populations.
options.B: revisionist economic history has substantially challenged the earlier, more benign framing of colonial trade by emphasizing the coercive political structures underlying it, without denying colonized populations’ genuine economic agency.
options.C: colonial trade patterns had no relationship whatsoever to contemporary global economic inequality.
options.D: the earlier, benign framing of colonial trade remains the most accurate account available.

questions.explanation: The passage’s careful structure — presenting revisionist evidence while explicitly rejecting the “cruder” version that denies agency entirely — matches this nuanced argument. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit third paragraph acknowledging “considerable, well-documented economic agency.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s final paragraph, which explicitly connects this history to “contemporary debates” about inequality. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s central, sustained critique of that framing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the revisionist scholarship’s key contribution was to:

options.A: prove that no colonial economic activity ever involved genuine market exchange.
options.B: take seriously the question of what coercive political conditions shaped the apparent structure of colonial trade.
options.C: argue that colonizing powers provided no infrastructure investment of any kind.
options.D: demonstrate that colonized populations had no interest in economic activity.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific reframing the passage attributes to the revisionist scholarship in the first paragraph. (A) overstates into an absolute the passage’s more measured claim about power asymmetries shaping, not eliminating, exchange. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s discussion of railway and port infrastructure investment (albeit built for extractive purposes). (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of agency and adaptation.

questions.stem: The passage’s discussion of infrastructure investment (paragraph 2) is used primarily to:

options.A: argue that colonizing powers were generous in developing colonized regions.
options.B: illustrate how infrastructure was designed to serve extraction rather than genuine internal regional economic development.
options.C: prove that railways had no economic function of any kind.
options.D: show that colonized regions had superior infrastructure to colonizing countries.

questions.explanation: This is exactly the point the example is used to support — infrastructure “designed overwhelmingly to move raw materials outward… rather than to connect and develop internal regional economies.” (A) directly contradicts the critical framing of the example. (C) misreads the example, which acknowledges railways had a function, just an extractive rather than developmental one. (D) is a claim never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The author addresses a potential objection to the revisionist view in paragraph 3 primarily by:

options.A: ignoring it entirely and refusing to engage with the counterargument.
options.B: acknowledging genuine economic agency existed while arguing this doesn’t rescue the earlier, more benign framing, since available opportunities were themselves shaped by coercion.
options.C: conceding that the revisionist view is entirely mistaken.
options.D: arguing that colonized populations had complete economic freedom throughout the colonial period.

questions.explanation: This precisely describes the passage’s careful, concessive-but-ultimately-unyielding argumentative move in paragraph 3. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s substantial, explicit engagement with the objection. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s continued defense of the revisionist framing after raising the objection. (D) is an extreme claim the passage explicitly avoids making.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “comparative advantage” most nearly refers to:

options.A: a military strategy used during colonial conquest.
options.B: an economic concept describing a region’s relative efficiency advantage in producing particular goods, used here to question whether trade patterns reflected this or were imposed.
options.C: a legal term describing property rights under colonial law.
options.D: a specific tax imposed by colonial administrations.

questions.explanation: This is the standard economic meaning being invoked and directly questioned throughout the passage — whether colonial specialization reflected genuine comparative advantage or was “actively and deliberately imposed.” (A), (C), and (D) are unrelated or incorrect senses not supported by the passage’s usage.

questions.stem: The passage’s central argument is that:

options.A: oral tradition is always more reliable than written records in every possible case.
options.B: both oral and written historical sources require the same kind of specific, source-critical scrutiny, rather than assuming written sources are inherently more reliable.
options.C: written records should be abandoned entirely in favor of oral history.
options.D: oral traditions from West African societies have never been checked against any independent evidence.

questions.explanation: The passage’s explicit conclusion — “the more useful methodological lesson… is not that either… deserve a blanket presumption of superior reliability” — matches this precisely. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit caution against treating them as “simply interchangeable” or claiming blanket superiority for oral tradition either. (C) is an extreme position never suggested anywhere in the passage. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of checking oral traditions “against independent written sources.”

questions.stem: According to the passage, the specific oral transmission methods described (paragraph 2) were designed to:

options.A: deliberately introduce variation into historical accounts over time.
options.B: catch and correct the kind of transmission errors a naive model of oral tradition would predict as inevitable.
options.C: prevent any written records from ever being created.
options.D: replace genealogical information with fictional narratives.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s stated purpose of these structured, redundant methods. (A) is the opposite of their described purpose — accuracy preservation, not deliberate variation. (C) and (D) are claims never made anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage identifies which specific vulnerability as unique to oral tradition, as compared to written records?

options.A: Oral traditions can never preserve genealogical information accurately.
options.B: Oral traditions, as living performed traditions, are susceptible to gradual reshaping to serve present political needs during ongoing performance.
options.C: Oral traditions are always immediately destroyed by colonial administrations.
options.D: Oral traditions cannot be cross-checked against any other source.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific vulnerability the passage attributes to oral tradition’s nature as a “living, actively performed” tradition. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s evidence of accurate genealogical preservation. (C) is an unsupported claim never made. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of cross-checking against written sources and archaeological evidence.

questions.stem: The final paragraph’s central claim is that treating “written” as inherently more reliable than “oral”:

options.A: is scientifically well-supported by all available evidence.
options.B: mistakenly conflates a source’s medium of transmission with its actual evidentiary reliability.
options.C: has never been questioned by any historian.
options.D: applies equally well to every society throughout history.

questions.explanation: This is the passage’s precise, explicit closing claim. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s sustained critique of this assumption throughout. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s extensive discussion of historians and anthropologists challenging this assumption. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s specific point that this correlation was particular to “the specific societies where modern academic historical scholarship first developed.”

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “epistemic authority” most nearly means:

options.A: legal power to enforce a written contract.
options.B: the presumed credibility or reliability granted to a source of knowledge.
options.C: the political power held by colonial administrations.
options.D: the physical durability of written documents compared to spoken words.

questions.explanation: In context (“written records have long enjoyed a kind of default epistemic authority”), the phrase refers to a presumed status of reliability or credibility as a knowledge source. (A) and (C) are unrelated senses involving legal or political power, not knowledge credibility. (D) narrows the term to a physical property, which is a separate point the passage makes elsewhere, not what “epistemic authority” itself means.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all museum holdings from colonized regions should be immediately and unconditionally returned.
options.B: examine the justifications museums have offered for retaining contested artifacts and the substantial counterarguments each has faced.
options.C: prove that repatriation movements have entirely failed to achieve any policy change.
options.D: argue that formerly colonized nations lack adequate infrastructure to preserve returned artifacts.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — presenting three distinct museum justifications, then substantial counterarguments to each, then evolving policy — matches this balanced, analytical purpose. (A) is a specific advocacy position never taken by the passage, which presents multiple perspectives without fully endorsing one. (C) is directly contradicted by the passage’s explicit discussion of “several prominent museums and national governments” shifting policy. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s discussion of this argument having “grown markedly weaker” given new infrastructure.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics argue the “universal museum” justification is weakened because:

options.A: it was formulated largely after most relevant acquisitions had already taken place, functioning as retroactive justification.
options.B: universal museums have never educated anyone about other cultures.
options.C: it is based entirely on forged historical documents.
options.D: no museum has ever used this argument in practice.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific critique the passage attributes to critics of this argument. (B) is an extreme claim never made in the passage, which doesn’t dispute the museums’ educational value generally, only the argument’s historical timing. (C) and (D) are unsupported claims never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the conservation-capacity argument has weakened over time primarily because:

options.A: all artifacts have become significantly more durable due to new preservation technology.
options.B: formerly colonized nations have increasingly built museum and conservation infrastructure capable of professional-standard preservation.
options.C: museums in Europe and North America have lost their own conservation capabilities.
options.D: international law now prohibits any form of artifact conservation.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific development the passage cites as weakening this argument. (A) misattributes the change to artifact durability rather than the actual cited cause (new infrastructure elsewhere). (C) and (D) are claims never made anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage characterizes the current, case-by-case repatriation approach as:

options.A: fully satisfying both restitution advocates and museum defenders.
options.B: satisfying few observers on either side completely, given differing concerns about pace, criteria, and precedent.
options.C: a complete failure that has resulted in zero artifact returns.
options.D: something no museum has actually attempted to implement.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit characterization of the current approach’s reception. (A) directly contradicts “satisfies few observers on either side… completely.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of “negotiated, case-by-case return of specific objects” actually occurring. (D) is directly contradicted by the same discussion of museums actively “shifting policy.”

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “provenance” most nearly means:

options.A: the current market value of an artifact.
options.B: the origin and subsequent history of ownership of an object.
options.C: the physical material an artifact is made from.
options.D: the museum currently displaying an artifact.

questions.explanation: This is the standard meaning of the term, matched by its context (“sorting any specific object’s actual provenance into one of these categories” of acquisition circumstance). (A), (C), and (D) are unrelated or incorrect senses not supported by the passage’s usage, which is specifically about acquisition history.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that language death is a purely natural, unproblematic process that requires no attention or concern.
options.B: explain the causes and consequences of language extinction, and distinguish between the related but distinct efforts of documentation and revitalization.
options.C: prove that Hebrew’s revival can be easily replicated for every endangered language worldwide.
options.D: argue that all state-mandated schooling should be immediately abolished.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — causes of language death, the case for its significance, documentation versus revitalization as distinct goals — matches this comprehensive, explanatory purpose. (A) is directly contradicted by the passage’s substantial case for “actively caring about this loss.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that this combination is “unlikely to be replicable at anything approaching the scale” needed generally. (D) is a policy position never suggested in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why might a language’s disappearance represent an irrecoverable loss?

options.A: Because all languages are grammatically identical to one another.
options.B: Because a language encodes accumulated cultural and cognitive knowledge that is often not straightforwardly translatable or recoverable once lost.
options.C: Because languages can always be perfectly reconstructed from written records alone.
options.D: Because linguists have never attempted to document endangered languages.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s stated case for the loss’s significance. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s discussion of genuinely different grammatical structures across languages. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that documentation does not fully recover what is lost. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s extensive discussion of expanding documentation efforts.

questions.stem: The passage distinguishes “documentation” from “revitalization” by noting that:

options.A: they are entirely unrelated processes with no connection to one another.
options.B: documentation preserves a linguistic record, while revitalization aims to restore or increase a language’s number of active, everyday speakers — a more difficult, distinct goal.
options.C: documentation is always more difficult to achieve than revitalization.
options.D: revitalization requires no political will or institutional resources.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit distinction between the two, made clear in the transition between paragraphs 3 and 4. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s statement that they are “frequently complementary and often pursued together in practice.” (C) directly reverses the passage’s clear framing of revitalization as “the more ambitious and considerably more difficult project.” (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit list of what revitalization requires.

questions.stem: The Hebrew example is used in the passage to:

options.A: prove that language revitalization is generally easy to achieve for any language.
options.B: illustrate a genuine, well-documented success in large-scale language revitalization, while the passage cautions this success is difficult to replicate broadly.
options.C: show that liturgical languages should never be used in everyday speech.
options.D: argue that Hebrew should be considered an endangered language today.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly frames this as a “genuinely inspiring success” immediately followed by an explicit caution about the difficulty of replicating the required conditions elsewhere. (A) directly contradicts this explicit caution about replicability. (C) misreads the example, which describes a shift from liturgical to everyday use as a success, not an argument against liturgical use itself. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s use of Hebrew as an example of successful revival, the opposite of an endangered language today.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “vernacular” most nearly means:

options.A: a formal, ceremonial style of writing used only in religious contexts.
options.B: the everyday, ordinary spoken language of a particular community.
options.C: a dead language no longer used by anyone.
options.D: a written alphabet system.

questions.explanation: In context (“Hebrew’s large-scale revival as an everyday spoken vernacular”), the term clearly refers to ordinary, everyday spoken language, explicitly contrasted with prior “liturgical and scholarly use.” (A) is close to the opposite of the intended meaning — vernacular contrasts with formal/liturgical use here. (C) directly contradicts the described revival into active use. (D) is an unrelated, incorrect sense of the word.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all modernist urban planning projects were secretly, deliberately designed to fail.
options.B: trace how observational critique of modernist urban renewal revealed the undervalued social function of dense, mixed-use neighborhoods, while noting this lesson remains incompletely applied.
options.C: prove that no urban planning has ever successfully improved any city.
options.D: advocate for the complete abolition of all future urban planning regulation.

questions.explanation: The passage’s arc — modernist confidence, the observational critique that followed, the “eyes on the street” explanation, and the incomplete, ongoing nature of the resulting shift — matches this analytical purpose precisely. (A) is an unsupported, uncharitable claim never made; the passage describes miscalibrated confidence, not deliberate sabotage. (C) overstates a critique of specific projects into a blanket claim never made. (D) is a specific policy position never suggested in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, “eyes on the street” refers to:

options.A: formal, government-installed security cameras.
options.B: the informal, low-level social surveillance generated naturally by mixed-use neighborhoods with steady foot traffic throughout the day.
options.C: a specific law requiring windows to face public streets.
options.D: a planning theory advocating for wider, car-oriented roads.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit definition of the term. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s specific description of this as “informal” and “unplanned,” distinct from formal security measures. (C) and (D) are unsupported, incorrect characterizations not given by the passage.

questions.stem: The monumental plaza example (paragraph 3) is used in the passage to:

options.A: show that all large public plazas are poorly designed and should never be built.
options.B: illustrate how a space lacking ongoing, informal reasons for people to be present can become functionally dead despite impressive planned design.
options.C: prove that office towers should never be built near public plazas.
options.D: demonstrate that architectural renderings are always inaccurate.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific point the example illustrates — the gap between planned appearance and actual, sustained use given the absence of “ongoing reason to actually be there.” (A) and (C) overstate the specific example into sweeping, general prohibitions never suggested. (D) misreads the example’s actual point, which is about use patterns, not rendering accuracy generally.

questions.stem: The passage’s final paragraph suggests that the shift toward mixed-use planning has been:

options.A: total and complete across all urban development globally.
options.B: influential in professional planning theory but incompletely applied in actual ongoing practice.
options.C: entirely rejected by contemporary urban planners.
options.D: irrelevant to how cities are currently being built.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit, hedged final assessment — influential “in principle” but not consistently applied “in the actual, ongoing practice.” (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that this “would… be an overstatement.” (C) and (D) both directly contradict the passage’s discussion of the critique’s substantial, ongoing influence on planning theory.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “sterile” (paragraph 2) most nearly means:

options.A: medically clean and free of germs.
options.B: lacking vitality, activity, or genuine social function.
options.C: biologically unable to reproduce.
options.D: extremely expensive to construct.

questions.explanation: In context (“functionally sterile despite their considerable design sophistication”), the word describes a lack of vibrant social use and function, not a literal medical or biological property. (A) and (C) are the word’s literal, unrelated senses not supported by this figurative context. (D) is an unsupported, unrelated meaning.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all first-person narratives in literature should be considered completely untrustworthy and therefore worthless.
options.B: examine how the unreliable narrator technique works craft-wise, and explore its deeper thematic significance beyond mere formal trickery.
options.C: prove that unreliable narrators are a recent literary invention with no historical precedent.
options.D: argue that third-person narration is always superior to first-person narration.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — explaining the craft challenge, the “gap” technique, and the deeper thematic payoff — matches this analytical, appreciative purpose. (A) overstates the passage’s actual, more nuanced point about narrative construction into a dismissive claim never made. (C) is a claim about historical origins never made or discussed in the passage. (D) is a comparison never made anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, an author who reveals a narrator’s unreliability “too heavily, too early” risks:

options.A: making the reader trust the narrator even more than intended.
options.B: causing the reader to disengage from the narrative voice and read the work as a decoding exercise rather than an immersive story.
options.C: making the novel too short to be published.
options.D: eliminating the need for any plot at all.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific risk the passage describes for over-signaling unreliability too early. (A) is the opposite outcome of what the passage describes. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported claims never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The term “the gap,” as used in the passage, refers to:

options.A: a plot hole or unresolved inconsistency the author failed to address.
options.B: the space between what a narrator explicitly claims and what other incidental details in the narrative inadvertently reveal.
options.C: the physical break between chapters in a novel.
options.D: the difference in page count between two competing editions of a book.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s stated definition of the term as used by literary critics. (A) misreads the term as an authorial flaw, when the passage frames it as a deliberate technique. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported meanings never suggested by the passage.

questions.stem: The passage’s final paragraph suggests that skillfully executed unreliable narration:

options.A: has no connection to how people understand their own lives and memories.
options.B: dramatizes, through narrative technique itself, the broader idea that all first-person accounts, including our own self-narratives, are inherently partial and constructed.
options.C: proves that all novels with unreliable narrators are objectively superior to those without.
options.D: is primarily valued for making novels more difficult to summarize.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit closing claim about the technique’s deeper significance. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit connection to “the internal narratives each of us constructs… about our own lives.” (C) and (D) are unsupported, overstated claims never made in the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “recontextualization” most nearly means:

options.A: the physical relocation of a story’s setting to a new place.
options.B: a reframing that changes how earlier information in a narrative should be understood.
options.C: a legal process for republishing an out-of-print book.
options.D: the translation of a text into a different language.

questions.explanation: In context (“a carefully earned recontextualization of everything that preceded it”), the term refers to a reveal that reshapes understanding of earlier narrative content. (A), (C), and (D) are unrelated, unsupported senses not matching the literary-critical context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that literary translation is impossible and should never be attempted.
options.B: examine the deep, structural challenges of literary translation and the competing theoretical frameworks developed to address them.
options.C: prove that domesticating translation is always the superior approach.
options.D: argue that only bilingual readers should be permitted to read translated literature.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — the fluency/fidelity paradox, the deeper-than-vocabulary nature of the challenge, and the domesticating/foreignizing framework — matches this analytical purpose. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s substantial, serious engagement with how translation is actually practiced and theorized, not dismissed as impossible. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that neither approach is “universally ‘correct.’” (D) is a position never suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, focusing the “untranslatability” discussion on isolated vocabulary examples:

options.A: fully captures the true nature and scope of the translation challenge.
options.B: somewhat understates the deeper, more pervasive nature of the challenge, which operates at every level of a text including syntax and connotation.
options.C: is a discussion translation theorists have entirely abandoned as irrelevant.
options.D: applies only to translations between closely related languages.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit critique of the narrower, vocabulary-focused framing. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s stated critique of this framing as understating the real challenge. (C) is directly contradicted, since the passage continues to engage with vocabulary examples as a real, if incomplete, part of the discussion. (D) is a claim never made anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage distinguishes “domesticating” from “foreignizing” translation by explaining that:

options.A: domesticating translation prioritizes natural readability, while foreignizing translation deliberately preserves linguistic and cultural strangeness.
options.B: foreignizing translation is always more accurate than domesticating translation.
options.C: domesticating translation was invented more recently than foreignizing translation.
options.D: the two approaches produce identical results in every case.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit definitional distinction between the two approaches. (B) is a claim never made — the passage explicitly avoids ranking one as universally superior. (C) is an unsupported historical claim never made in the passage. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s entire framing of these as genuinely distinct approaches.

questions.stem: The passage’s final paragraph suggests that the choice between translation approaches should account for:

options.A: only the personal preference of the individual translator.
options.B: the specific power relationship between the source and target languages and cultures, among other contextual factors.
options.C: exclusively the commercial marketability of the translated work.
options.D: nothing beyond strict grammatical accuracy.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific factor the passage highlights as “perhaps most importantly and most easily overlooked.” (A), (C), and (D) all narrow the passage’s multi-factor, explicitly broader consideration (“purpose,” “readership,” “power relationship”) down to a single, unsupported criterion.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “connotative weight” most nearly refers to:

options.A: the literal, dictionary definition of a word.
options.B: the additional associative and emotional meaning a word carries beyond its literal definition, from its history of use.
options.C: the number of syllables in a given word.
options.D: the grammatical category (noun, verb, etc.) a word belongs to.

questions.explanation: In context (“the connotative weight a given word… carries by virtue of its accumulated prior use… within that language’s own literary tradition”), the phrase clearly refers to associative meaning beyond literal definition. (A) directly contradicts “connotative,” which specifically means beyond the literal/denotative meaning. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported senses not matched by the passage’s context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all literary criticism is entirely subjective and therefore worthless.
options.B: present two conflicting conceptions of critical authority, examine the difficulties with each taken to an extreme, and propose a more defensible middle position.
options.C: prove that credentialed critics are always more insightful than general readers.
options.D: argue that popular and genre fiction should never be taken seriously by critics.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — presenting the credentialist view, the suspicious/relativist counter-view, difficulties with both extremes, and a proposed middle position — matches this balanced, analytical purpose precisely. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s final paragraph, which explicitly argues against pure relativism. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s substantial critique of pure credentialism. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit criticism of dismissing such traditions as a flaw of traditional criticism.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the “credentialist” view of critical authority risks, in its extreme form:

options.A: becoming too open to entirely new and unfamiliar forms of literature.
options.B: calcifying into a closed system that fails to recognize innovation unresembling already-established, validated forms.
options.C: eliminating the need for any formal literary education.
options.D: treating all works of literature as equally valuable.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific risk the passage attributes to this view taken to its logical extreme. (A) is the opposite of the described risk, which is excessive closedness, not openness. (C) directly contradicts the credentialist view’s actual emphasis on formal training. (D) describes the opposing, relativist view’s risk, not this one.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a purely relativist view of aesthetic judgment struggles to account for:

options.A: the fact that all critics agree completely on every judgment.
options.B: the persistent, widely shared intuition that some aesthetic judgments are better reasoned and more perceptive than others.
options.C: the existence of formal literary education programs.
options.D: the popularity of genre fiction among general readers.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific difficulty the passage identifies for the relativist position. (A) is an overstated claim never made — critics disagreeing is compatible with the passage’s point, which is about a shared underlying intuition, not unanimous agreement. (C) and (D) are unrelated to the specific difficulty being described.

questions.stem: The passage’s proposed “middle position” characterizes critical authority as:

options.A: an unquestionable credential immune to any challenge.
options.B: entirely illusory and without any genuine basis.
options.C: earned, situated expertise that remains open to challenge and revision by better-reasoned competing accounts.
options.D: something that depends solely on a critic’s job title.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit description of the proposed middle position. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that this expertise “remains itself always open to challenge… rather than being treated… as simply final.” (B) describes the relativist extreme the middle position explicitly rejects. (D) is an unsupported, overly narrow characterization not given by the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “calcifying” most nearly means:

options.A: becoming increasingly flexible and adaptable over time.
options.B: hardening or becoming rigid and resistant to change.
options.C: dissolving completely and ceasing to exist.
options.D: growing rapidly in size or influence.

questions.explanation: In context (“risks calcifying into a closed, self-referential system”), the word describes a process of rigidification, matching the described risk of a system becoming closed and resistant to recognizing new forms. (A) is the opposite of the intended meaning. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported senses not matching this context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that genre fiction is objectively superior to literary fiction in every case.
options.B: examine the literary/genre fiction hierarchy, present challenges to it, and note the hierarchy’s persistence despite growing critical reassessment.
options.C: prove that no meaningful distinction between literary and genre fiction has ever existed.
options.D: advocate for eliminating all genre categories from bookstores and libraries.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — describing the hierarchy, presenting two distinct lines of critique, and noting uneven but real institutional change alongside persistence — matches this analytical purpose. (A) is an extreme reversal never argued by the passage, which questions the hierarchy without simply inverting it. (C) overstates the passage’s actual, more measured claim about the boundary being unstable and retrospectively constructed, not entirely nonexistent. (D) is a policy position never suggested in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the first line of criticism against the literary/genre hierarchy points out that:

options.A: genre fiction has never been commercially successful.
options.B: many now-canonized literary classics were originally marketed and received as genre fiction.
options.C: literary fiction did not exist as a category until the twenty-first century.
options.D: all genre fiction eventually becomes literary fiction over time.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific historical point the passage attributes to this line of criticism. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s implicit point, since the examples given were popular works, and is unrelated to the specific critique cited. (C) and (D) are unsupported, overstated claims never made in the passage.

questions.stem: The mystery novel example (paragraph 3) is used in the passage to:

options.A: prove that mystery novels are more artistically valuable than literary novels.
options.B: illustrate that genre fiction can demonstrate its own considerable, differently-oriented craft, not straightforwardly inferior to literary fiction’s different kind of craft.
options.C: show that mystery novels never contain any suspense or narrative resolution.
options.D: argue that literary prizes should exclusively reward mystery novels going forward.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific, carefully balanced point the example is used to illustrate — “neither straightforwardly inferior nor superior… but simply differently oriented.” (A) overstates the passage’s careful, balanced claim into a one-sided superiority claim it explicitly avoids making. (C) directly contradicts the passage’s description of these craft elements being present and well-executed. (D) is an extreme policy position never suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The phrase “transcends the genre,” as discussed in the final paragraph, is presented by the author as:

options.A: a phrase that has entirely disappeared from contemporary critical writing.
options.B: a seemingly complimentary phrase that nonetheless reveals and perpetuates the underlying hierarchy it claims to move beyond.
options.C: proof that the literary/genre hierarchy has been fully resolved and no longer exists.
options.D: an insult that no genre author would ever want applied to their work.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit, nuanced characterization of the phrase’s function. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s description of it as “genuinely common” in current use. (C) directly contradicts the entire point of citing the phrase as evidence of the hierarchy’s persistence. (D) is an unsupported claim about author reception never discussed in the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “valorized” most nearly means:

options.A: financially devalued or made cheaper.
options.B: assigned or celebrated with special value, worth, or prestige.
options.C: legally prohibited or banned.
options.D: translated into a foreign language.

questions.explanation: In context (“the specific, valorized hallmarks of literary fiction”), the word describes qualities given elevated status or prestige within the described hierarchy. (A) is close to the opposite of the intended meaning. (C) and (D) are unrelated, unsupported senses not matching the context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that all humans are equally overconfident in every domain of judgment without exception.
options.B: distinguish between three related but analytically separable forms of overconfidence, and identify feedback quality as a key factor moderating their occurrence.
options.C: prove that professional weather forecasters never make inaccurate predictions.
options.D: argue that overconfidence is a fixed personality trait some people simply have more of than others.

questions.explanation: The passage’s structure — defining overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision separately, then identifying feedback quality as the key moderating factor — matches this analytical purpose precisely. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit discussion of domain-specific variability. (C) overstates a claim never made — the passage discusses lower rates of overconfidence in this field, not the elimination of all forecasting error. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that overconfidence is “less a single fixed personality trait… and more a systematic, predictable cognitive tendency” shaped by context.

questions.stem: According to the passage, “overplacement” specifically refers to:

options.A: believing one’s own performance is better than it objectively is, in absolute terms.
options.B: believing one is better than other people specifically, relative to a comparison group.
options.C: expressing excessive certainty about the accuracy of a specific belief or estimate.
options.D: the tendency to change one’s mind frequently based on new evidence.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit definition, distinguished clearly from the other two forms. (A) describes “overestimation,” a distinct, separately defined term. (C) describes “overprecision,” also separately and distinctly defined. (D) is an unrelated concept never discussed in the passage.

questions.stem: The driving skill example (paragraph 3) is used in the passage to illustrate:

options.A: that all three forms of overconfidence always occur together in the same person.
options.B: that a person can avoid one form of overconfidence (overplacement) in a domain while still exhibiting another (overprecision) in that same domain.
options.C: that driving is the most dangerous activity most people regularly engage in.
options.D: that professional drivers are less overconfident than amateur drivers.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific point the example is constructed to illustrate — the domain-specific dissociation between the different forms of overconfidence. (A) is the opposite of what the example demonstrates. (C) and (D) are unrelated claims never made using this example.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that long-range political and economic forecasting shows relatively higher rates of overconfidence primarily because:

options.A: political and economic forecasters are less intelligent than chess players.
options.B: feedback in this domain is often delayed, ambiguous, or easily rationalized away after an inaccurate prediction.
options.C: political and economic events are entirely random and unpredictable.
options.D: forecasters in this domain receive no financial compensation for their predictions.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific mechanism the passage identifies for this domain’s comparatively higher overconfidence. (A) is an unsupported, uncharitable claim never made in the passage. (C) overstates a claim never made — the passage discusses feedback quality, not a claim about total unpredictability. (D) is an unrelated, unsupported claim never discussed.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “moderating factor” most nearly means:

options.A: a factor that completely eliminates a phenomenon under all circumstances.
options.B: a factor that influences the strength or occurrence of a phenomenon without being its sole cause.
options.C: a person who mediates a formal debate or discussion.
options.D: a financial regulation imposed by a government body.

questions.explanation: In context (“the single most consistent and well-replicated moderating factor”), the phrase refers to a variable that shapes the degree to which overconfidence occurs, matching standard usage in psychological research. (A) overstates the term into complete elimination, which the passage doesn’t claim. (C) and (D) are unrelated senses of “moderator/moderating” not supported by this specific research context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: prove that institutional trust has increased steadily across all wealthy democracies in recent decades.
options.B: document the pattern of declining institutional trust, examine its uneven distribution and competing explanations, and note its real-world consequences and unresolved interpretation.
options.C: argue that scientific institutions are the least trustworthy of all major institutions.
options.D: advocate for the immediate abolition of all national governments.

questions.explanation: The passage’s comprehensive structure — the pattern, its unevenness, competing explanations, consequences, and an explicitly unresolved final question — matches this analytical purpose precisely. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s central finding of a “sustained, measurable decline.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s statement that scientific institutions have “held up somewhat better on average” compared to other tracked institutions. (D) is a policy position never suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the decline in trust toward national government is best characterized as:

options.A: uniform and identical in pace across every wealthy democracy studied.
options.B: closely correlated with specific national events like scandals or policy failures, rather than a single uniform global trend.
options.C: entirely unrelated to any specific historical events.
options.D: less severe than the decline in trust toward scientific institutions.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit characterization of this specific decline’s pattern. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement that pace and severity “vary considerably by country.” (C) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit correlation with “specific, identifiable national events.” (D) directly reverses the passage’s comparative claim, which states government trust “declined more sharply” than most other categories.

questions.stem: The passage identifies which of the following as a proposed explanation for declining institutional trust?

options.A: A global decrease in literacy rates across wealthy democracies.
options.B: Increased information access making institutional failures and misconduct more visible than in earlier eras.
options.C: A decline in the total number of institutions operating worldwide.
options.D: Increased trust in scientific expertise specifically.

questions.explanation: This is explicitly listed as one of the passage’s proposed explanations. (A) and (C) are claims never made anywhere in the passage. (D) is the opposite of a proposed cause — it describes an outcome, and one the passage actually complicates rather than straightforwardly affirms.

questions.stem: The passage’s final paragraph presents which of the following as a genuinely unresolved question?

options.A: Whether institutional trust has declined at all in recent decades.
options.B: Whether declining trust reflects a rational response to institutional failure or a less rational, self-reinforcing cultural drift.
options.C: Whether political scientists study democratic institutions.
options.D: Whether public health guidance exists in any country.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the specific question the passage explicitly frames as “genuinely and seriously contested… without any clear scholarly consensus yet in sight.” (A) is not in dispute in the passage — the decline itself is presented as an established finding, not a contested question. (C) and (D) are not genuine questions raised anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “monocausal” most nearly means:

options.A: attributing an outcome to a single cause, rather than multiple contributing factors.
options.B: relating to money or financial systems specifically.
options.C: occurring only once in history, without repetition.
options.D: impossible to measure using any research method.

questions.explanation: In context (“rather than any single, monocausal explanation”), the word clearly means attributing an effect to one sole cause, distinguished explicitly from a multi-factor explanation. (B), (C), and (D) are unrelated or incorrect senses not supported by the passage’s context.

questions.stem: The passage’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: prove that the placebo effect can cure any disease, including cancer, if a patient believes strongly enough.
options.B: trace how understanding of the placebo effect has evolved from dismissive skepticism to serious study of its specific, bounded neurobiological mechanisms.
options.C: argue that all clinical trials should be discontinued because of the placebo effect.
options.D: prove that deceiving patients is always ethically justified if it produces a placebo benefit.

questions.explanation: The passage’s arc — early dismissive framing, physiological evidence, the pattern of variation by condition type, and the open-label finding — matches this evolutionary, analytical purpose precisely. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit statement about “minimal to no measurable effect” on objective measures like tumor size. (C) is a position never suggested anywhere in the passage. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s explicit description of deception as “seriously and legitimately problematic.”

questions.stem: According to the passage, early explanations of the placebo effect tended to:

options.A: treat it as a genuine, well-documented physiological phenomenon with measurable brain changes.
options.B: dismissively attribute it to patient suggestibility or self-deception, rather than a genuine physiological phenomenon.
options.C: immediately recognize it as equally effective for both subjective and objective medical outcomes.
options.D: recommend it as a first-line treatment for cancer.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit description of the earlier, more dismissive framing. (A) describes the later, more rigorous understanding the passage says developed subsequently, not the early view. (C) and (D) are claims never made anywhere in the passage about the early explanations specifically.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that placebo effects are strongest for which category of medical conditions?

options.A: Conditions substantially mediated by subjective, self-reported experience, such as pain and self-assessed quality of life.
options.B: Conditions measured exclusively through objective physiological markers like tumor size.
options.C: Viral infections with a directly measurable viral load.
options.D: All medical conditions equally, without meaningful variation.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit description of where the effect shows “comparatively strong, well-replicated effects.” (B) and (C) directly describe the categories the passage explicitly says show “minimal to no measurable effect.” (D) directly contradicts the passage’s central point about the effect’s magnitude varying “dramatically” by condition type.

questions.stem: The “open-label placebo” finding is significant, according to the passage, because it:

options.A: proves that patients can never be told the truth about their treatment.
options.B: complicates the earlier assumption that deception or uncertainty was strictly necessary for the placebo effect to occur, opening an ethical path to harnessing the effect.
options.C: shows that placebo effects only occur when patients are actively deceived.
options.D: demonstrates that the placebo effect has no relationship to patient belief at all.

questions.explanation: This is precisely the passage’s explicit description of the finding’s significance. (A) directly contradicts the passage’s actual point, which is about honest disclosure still producing an effect. (C) is the exact opposite of what this finding demonstrates. (D) directly contradicts the passage’s overall framing of the effect as related to expectation and belief throughout.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, “mediated by” most nearly means:

options.A: resolved through formal legal mediation or arbitration.
options.B: brought about or influenced through the operation of a particular process or mechanism.
options.C: completely unrelated to or independent of.
options.D: broadcast publicly through mass media channels.

questions.explanation: In context (“conditions substantially mediated by subjective, self-reported experience”), the phrase means these conditions are significantly shaped or influenced through this specific channel. (A) and (D) are unrelated senses of “mediate/media” not supported by this context. (C) is close to the opposite of the intended meaning.

passages.title: Free Will and Determinism
paras: The question of whether human beings possess free will has occupied philosophers for millennia, but the terms of the debate shifted decisively with the rise of modern neuroscience. Beginning in the 1980s, experiments using brain imaging suggested that neural activity associated with a decision could be detected before subjects reported being consciously aware of having decided anything at all. To many observers, this seemed to settle a very old question in a very unflattering way: the feeling of choosing, on this reading, is not the cause of our actions but a kind of after-the-fact narration the brain supplies once the decision has already been made elsewhere.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat this finding as more conclusive than it is. The original experiments involved trivial, unplanned motor actions — pressing a button whenever the urge struck — and it remains deeply unclear whether the same mechanism governs deliberate, reasoned choices, the kind we actually care about when we ask whether someone is morally responsible for a decision. Critics have also pointed out that detecting neural activity slightly before conscious awareness does not prove that activity determined the outcome; it may simply reflect the brain assembling the conditions under which a conscious decision will shortly be made, much as a kitchen can be “getting ready” for a decision about what to cook without that preparation dictating the final choice.

What the debate has usefully clarified, even without resolving the underlying metaphysical question, is that “free will” was never a single, well-defined concept to begin with. Philosophers distinguish at minimum between a strong libertarian sense — the idea that our choices are genuinely uncaused by prior physical states, a notion increasingly difficult to reconcile with a physical universe governed by cause and effect — and a compatibilist sense, which holds that free will simply means acting according to one’s own reasons and desires, without external coercion, regardless of whether those reasons and desires were themselves caused by prior physical states. Under the compatibilist definition, the neuroscience findings are almost beside the point: of course your brain state causes your decision, because your brain state simply is you making the decision, not some external puppeteer pulling your strings.

This distinction matters enormously for how society ought to think about responsibility and punishment. If free will requires an impossible kind of uncaused causation, then strict moral responsibility becomes incoherent, and punishment can only be justified on forward-looking grounds — deterrence, rehabilitation, incapacitation — never on the backward-looking notion that someone “deserved” it. If, instead, the compatibilist definition is the one that actually matters for everyday moral life, then the neuroscience findings, however interesting, leave our ordinary practices of praise and blame largely undisturbed, since those practices were never premised on the libertarian notion in the first place. The persistence of this disagreement, more than a century after the philosophical groundwork was laid and decades after the neuroscience began, suggests that what looks like an empirical dispute is, underneath, a disagreement about which questions are even the right ones to be asking.

passages.title: The Nature of Consciousness
paras: Among the many unresolved problems in philosophy of mind, none has proven more stubbornly resistant to progress than what is often called the “hard problem” of consciousness. The distinction, first articulated with particular clarity in the 1990s, separates the “easy” problems of consciousness — explaining how the brain processes information, integrates sensory data, or produces behavior — from the genuinely hard problem: explaining why any of that physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all. Why does the processing of red wavelengths of light feel like something — why is there a subjective quality to seeing red, rather than the information simply being processed in the dark, so to speak, with no one home to experience it?

The “easy” problems are not actually easy in any everyday sense; they represent some of the most sophisticated ongoing work in neuroscience. But they are easy in the specific philosophical sense that we can, in principle, imagine a complete answer: a full account of neural mechanisms that produces a full account of the behavior in question. The hard problem resists this kind of resolution because no matter how complete a mechanistic account becomes, a further question always seems to remain: why should this mechanism be accompanied by experience rather than occurring, as philosophers put it, “in the dark”? A being that processed all the same information, produced all the same behavior, but had no inner experience at all — a so-called philosophical zombie — is, at least conceivably, imaginable, which suggests that experience is not simply identical to or automatically entailed by the physical processing itself.

Not everyone accepts that the hard problem is genuinely hard, or even that it is a coherent problem at all. Some philosophers argue that the intuition driving it — the sense that a mechanistic explanation could never fully account for subjective experience — is itself a kind of illusion produced by the very cognitive architecture we’re trying to explain, and that as our mechanistic understanding deepens, the intuition that “something is left out” will simply fade away, the way many other apparent mysteries have dissolved under sufficiently detailed explanation. Others go further, arguing that talk of subjective experience “over and above” physical processes smuggles in a dualism that careful philosophical analysis should dissolve rather than accommodate.

What makes the debate genuinely difficult to adjudicate, rather than merely difficult to resolve, is that it may be impossible, even in principle, to gather evidence that would settle it either way. Behavioral and neural evidence can tell us a great deal about the structure and function of experience, but by the hard problem’s own definition, no amount of third-person, externally observable data can directly confirm or rule out the presence of first-person, subjective experience in a system other than oneself. This asymmetry — between what science observes from the outside and what consciousness, if it exists, is experienced from the inside — is precisely why the problem has outlasted so many other disputes in philosophy of mind that seemed, at one time, equally intractable.

passages.title: Moral Luck
paras: Ordinary moral judgment assumes that we should be held responsible only for what is within our control. Yet a striking feature of how we actually judge one another, first systematically examined by philosophers in the late 1970s, is that outcomes entirely outside an agent’s control routinely affect how harshly we judge them — a phenomenon now known as “moral luck.” Consider two drivers, both momentarily distracted while checking a phone, both running equally significant red lights. One street is empty; nothing happens. The other has a child crossing at exactly the wrong moment. We judge the second driver far more harshly than the first, often holding them criminally liable in a way we never would the first — despite the fact that the two drivers behaved identically, made identical choices, and differed only in a matter of pure chance entirely outside either one’s control.
